speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that the co-chairmen of the Geneva conference have now reached agreement on the steps to be taken aimed at bringing about a settlement in Laos. Yesterday, April 24, the governments of the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union issued an appeal for an immediate cease fire and called on all military authorities, parties and organizations in Laos to stop fighting and to enter into negotiations about arrangements for the cease fire.
Simultaneously the co-chairmen sent a message to the Prime Minister of India stating that they had called for a cease fire and proposing that he convene the international supervisory commission for Laos in New Delhi. It was the view of the co-chairmen that the commission will, in the first instance -and I quote from their joint message of April 24-
-discuss the question of the tasks and functions which should be allotted to it after the
cease fire in Laos, and will present an appropriate report to the co-chairmen who will consider the commission's report and give it directions on going to Laos to carry out the work of controlling the cease fire.
The co-chairmen have also agreed that an international conference should meet in Geneva on May 12 to discuss a settlement of the Laotian problem. The countries invited to this conference are those which attended the Geneva conference of 1954; the United Kingdom, the Soviet union, the United States, communist China, France, North Viet Nam, South Viet Nam, Cambodia and Laos; in addition, the members of the international supervisory commission, Canada, India and Poland; and two of the neighbouring countries, Thailand and Burma. All fourteen have been invited to send representatives. This membership follows that proposed by the chief of state of Cambodia, Prince Sihanouk, on January 1 of this year.
Yesterday morning I saw the ambassador of the Soviet union and the acting high commissioner for the United Kingdom, as representatives of the co-chairmen, and received from them the text of the invitation to the conference and a copy of the appeal for a cease-fire and of the message from Lord Home and Mr. Gromyko to Mr. Nehru. Last evening I received from Mr. Nehru a message requesting the government of Canada to nominate its representative on the commission and proposing that the first meeting of the commission should be held in New Delhi on Friday next, April 28.
I think the house will agree that the arrangements worked out between the co-chairmen, including the call for an immediate cease-fire to be effective before the international conference begins its work, constitute an important step toward the restoration of peace to Laos.
In response to the proposal that the commission should meet at once in New Delhi, I have named Mr. Leon Mayrand as Canadian member of the commission. Mr. Mayrand, who was our representative on the Laos commission in 1954-55, is at present our ambassador in Rome, and will be en route to New Delhi at the present time; at any rate. Mr. Mayrand will be assisted by Mr. d'Iberville Fortier of the Department of External Affairs, at present our representative on the commission in Cambodia, and by Brigadier P. S. Cooper of the Canadian army as senior military adviser, as well as by various other advisers.

Steps Towards Settlement in Laos
The Canadian government also accepts the invitation to attend the conference on Laos in Geneva. I expect to lead the Canadian delegation in the opening stages of the conference, which of course will follow almost immediately after the ministerial meeting of the North Atlantic council in Oslo which is scheduled to take place from May 8 to May 10 inclusive. The alternate head of the Canadian delegation to the conference will be Mr. C. A. Ronning, the Canadian high commissioner in India, whose long and distinguished service to Canada in Asia will be familiar to members of this house. He will be assisted by Mr. P. A. Bridle, our ambassador in Turkey, who was Canadian commissioner in Laos in 1955-56, and by civilian and military advisers with experience on the commissions.
By leave of the house Mr. Speaker, I should like to have the texts of the three documents, issued yesterday by the co-chairmen, and the text of the message from the prime minister of India, printed as an appendix to today's Hansard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the minister the consent which he requests?

Agreed.
[Editor's note: for text of documents referred to above, see appendix.1

Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is the first intervention in which the minister has been in a position to report progress regarding this regrettable situation in Laos. The proposal of the cochairmen, the foreign ministers of the Soviet union and the United Kingdom, as communicated to Canada and other members of the international truce supervisory commission, is of a threefold character, I would gather from what the minister has said; first of all, there is an agreement on a cease-fire; second, steps taken in Delhi for reactivation of the international supervisory commission; and third, there is to be a conference originally proposed by Prince Sihanouk of Cambodia of the Geneva and other powers.
It will be recalled that Canada, as a member of the commission which was set up by the Geneva accord in 1954, took the position that the commission could not be reactivated in the absence of the consent of the royal government of Laos. The minister did not mention whether that permission has now been extended, but I assume it is now the case that the royal government has consented to having the commission reactivated and assuming responsibilities in Vientiane. The reactivation of the commission is something that has been proposed now for some time, notably


by the country represented by the chairman of the commission, namely India.
The house was happy to be assured by the Secretary of State for External Affairs some months ago that if the commission had not been reactivated, notwithstanding reports to the contrary which emanated from India, the responsibility was not that of Canada. But this is not the place to engage in polemics; perhaps tomorrow further elucidation will be given by the minister as to this particular. The minister mentioned that the commission is going to have a preliminary meeting in New Delhi. I am sure he will agree that the record of achievement of this commission, particularly in Vientiane, more so perhaps than the commission in Viet Nam and Cambodia, has demonstrated its capacity for effectiveness in maintaining the peace.
The proposal for a conference of the Geneva and other powers does not come to the minister as a surprise because I think in January of this year he himself had proposed that this might be one of the ways of providing for a settlement of this very difficult situation in an area that is so vital to the peace of Asia and as a consequence to the peace of the world. The conference itself is now to have more participating nations than the conference of 1954. This time Canada is to be a full member along with Thailand and Burma, countries that certainly have a very direct interest in what evolves in that part of old Indo-China. In 1954 Canada was-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And India and Poland.

-a member of the international supervisory commission, along with India and Poland. Canada was not formally a member of that portion of the Geneva conference in 1954 that dealt with Indo-China, but she was represented there by the present Leader of the Opposition in respect of matters that had particular bearing on Korea. It is of interest to know that Mr. Chester Ronning, our Indian high commissioner in India, who had experience at that conference, will be at this new conference to assist the minister in the very important deliberations that will now affect Canada and other nations vitally and directly. The presence of Mr. Leon Mayrand as our representative on the international supervisory commission likewise would seem to be a wise appointment, in the light of his experience in 1954 on the commission in Laos.
We can only hope, Mr. Speaker, that the agreement between the co-chairmen, now confirmed by the three countries on the supervisory commission, will help to restore peace in an area that affects not only India and the other countries of south and southeast

Asia but all the nations of the world, particularly at this very difficult time when there has set in such a deterioration in international affairs. One can only hope that it is not too late to repair for that country and for the peace of the world, situations that have been allowed to evolve during the course of the last year when the interests of the west and of other nations concerned seemingly have been very seriously affected as a result of the fighting in Laos.

Mr. Speaker, while on occasions we differ from the minister, we know of his serious concern for those problems which face the world today. We notice that whenever he has an opportunity to announce some good news he does so with relish.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that, in view of recent events and the possibility surrounding them, we in this group were relieved and delighted to hear of the agreement that has been effected between Mr. Harold Macmillan of Great Britain and Mr. Khrushchev representing the U.S.S.R. Regardless of all the dark clouds surrounding us at this time, and the fears that arise on occasion, it does demonstrate what can be done when persons representing the western world in the right frame of mind, the right spirit and with the right purpose do what they can to reach agreement. In the opinion of this group this demonstrates the value of the type of persons in such negotiations who can keep their feet on the ground when everybody else is losing their balance.
We are very pleased to hear that Mr. Chester Ronning, our high commissioner in India, is going to be associated with this conference. His ability, his experience and his record are sufficient to indicate that his assistance and contribution to this conference will be to the credit of Canada and for the welfare of all concerned with restoring peace in this portion of the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house briefly of the promulgation of an amendment to the gold bullion regulations pursuant to the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act, revising the rate structure charged by the Royal Canadian Mint and the Bank of Canada in respect of gold bullion operations. The new charges are being instituted following a cost and revenue analysis of gold bullion operations. The new rate structure represents the first revision of mint charges in 30 years.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Generally speaking, melting, assaying and refining charges are being increased and handling charges-that is charges for the marketing of the gold outside Canada by the Bank of Canada-packing and storing charges are being reduced. The new rates for assaying and refining are comparable to United States mint charges; the reduced rates for handling, packing and storing more closely represent the actual cost of the service provided. The net effect of the revision will generally represent some saving to gold producers, the exception being suppliers of low grade ores.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has viewed and still views with deep concern the military insurrection which is taking place in Algeria against the lawful government of France. ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy policies. I do not know what the mover of the amendment had in mind when he made that statement, because it is somewhat ambiguous. Canada is a great trading nation; our export trade is most important, and I do not think any minister of trade and commerce has exerted himself more in developing this trade than the minister who now holds that portfolio.
Further on the amendment refers to a vigorous program to promote an expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries, and to encouraging the development of the Atlantic economic community. All I can say is that the mover of this amendment was a member of the former Liberal regime which held office for some 22 years, and I think the people of Canada, on reflection, will well remember the policies pursued by that government with regard to the development of our secondary industries. I do not think I need say any more in that regard.
I have spoken at some length about the development of the Atlantic economic community. This government, as I have said before, has gone a long way in participating in the economic development of the western world. We have now gone as far as any other country in the Atlantic world, by which I mean western Europe and North America. No other country has gone further. Having been associate members of O.E.E.C. we are now full members of O.E.C.D., an organization in which the countries of western Europe and North America are placing great hope. .
Therefore, in view of the arguments I made last night and those I have added today I do not think it is possible for me to support either the amendment moved by the hon. member for Laurier or the subamendment put forward on behalf of the C.C.F. party.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Speaking on this amendment I do not wish, at least at this stage, to go into the arguments raised by the hon. member who has just preceded me, except to say this in regard to his last remarks during which he said the record of the Liberal administration would speak for itself. Well, we are very content to let the record stand, and it will show that during that period secondary industries developed spectacularly in this country under the great industrial leadership of Right Hon. C. D. Howe, and developed without the sacrifice of our export industries, which increased steadily and continually during that period. If the record of the present government were comparable in any respect to that we would not be supporting this amendment today.


This amendment speaks for itself, and the attitude taken toward it by spokesmen on the government side speaks for itself. That attitude, as taken in this debate, makes it quite clear that the government will have nothing to do with the development of what is referred to in this amendment as an Atlantic economic community, which is the hope of the future for the Atlantic countries; an Atlantic economic community with a minimum of obstructions and restrictions and a maximum of exchange among its members.
This is a serious amendment dealing with a very important and serious subject. Unfortunately, for reasons which the minister will appreciate, I was not in the house yesterday to listen to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I might have been in the house Monday of last week to listen to him but he could not have been here then, so we made a mutually agreeable arrangement, or I believe it was mutually agreeable.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: You missed a flamboyant speech.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
I have had the privilege, although some would consider it a dubious one, of reading the minister's speech. In so far as it seemed to be concerned with a carefully thought out argument and memorandum on certain trade matters it was perhaps not unimpressive, even though we may not have agreed with it; but when the minister got out on his own, out of the field of trade and into polemics he was not very impressive. He indicated that this particular amendment was designed, if it had any purpose at all, to lay down a policy which would provide for jobs, as he put it, in Birmingham, Turin, Toledo and Detroit, at the expense of jobs in Canada. The producers of newsprint, lumber and agricultural products, and of fish and other primary products, know perfectly well, as the minister ought to know, that if there are not jobs in Turin, Birmingham, Detroit and Toledo there will not be jobs in Canada.
Embodied in this amendment is the policy of having jobs both abroad and in Canada; we will have more jobs in Canada because there are jobs and purchasing power abroad. The minister himself, who sometimes speaks from both sides of his mouth on this matter in a manner which I know he will forgive me if I characterize as rather immature and unsophisticated, said in this house as late as April 18, quoting from a speech he made in Toronto on February 7, 1961:
Some people say the government should give greater protection to industry by raising tariffs against imports. Those who make this suggestion should realize that those against whom they would

have us raise tariffs are also our customers for the exports on which we rely so heavily for our economic well-being.
Whether they are in Turin, Birmingham, Toledo or Detroit they are also our customers for exports on which we rely so heavily for our economic well-being. The minister also said in the same speech:
They must also realize that one out of every four Canadians is employed in either producing for, or shipping to, the export market.
One out of every four Canadians, according to the minister, is employed in either producing for or shipping to the export market. The minister said yesterday that the policy of his government is full employment. If that is it, then they have failed to carry out that policy when there are 705,000 or more unemployed. If full employment is the policy of the government it will not be accomplished by rejecting motions for the removal of obstructions to trade and encouragement of the expansion of trade because, as the minister puts it, one out of every four people in this country depends on exports for his livelihood.
Then the minister descended from what I have characterized as immaturity to what I can only characterize, and I know he will understand if I try to find another word to describe that which is even more superficial than immature, as drivel, when he had the following to say, as reported at page 3949 of Hansard for April 24, 1961:
They-
That is the Liberal party.
-want them-
That is the foreigners on whom we are relying for exports.
-to pour cheap goods into Canada to put Canadians out of work and to have mass unemployment, so that they can go to the people at the next election and say "Elect us and we will save you from your doom".
That statement of the purposes and motives of the Liberal party is what I characterize in this particular argument as drivel; which, of course, is what it is.
This particular amendment deals primarily with external trade. I intend to consider certain aspects of the amendment, some of which were discussed by the hon. gentleman who preceded me. I refer to those aspects which concern the possibilities of meeting some of our external trade problems in the world in which we live today by building up, as the only satisfactory solution to these problems, however it may be misunderstood or mischaracterized by hon. gentlemen opposite, an Atlantic trade area with maximum trade and minimum restrictions.
25. 1961
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
The situation has changed drastically in the world, in our country and on this continent since 1911, the days of reciprocity, to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce seems to relate our policies of today on external trade. That is an indication of how unable or unwilling he has been to grasp and understand what we are putting forward. It would be very wrong, unwise and indeed harmful for us to think in this country of trade problems, trade opportunities and trade circumstances in the light of 1911. Trade barriers, trade obstructions and indeed the whole concept of free trade itself should not be thought of in terms of 50 years ago, when tariffs were about the only thing that really mattered in this field.
The situation is very different now. Since those relatively simple days of external trade there have been growing up over the years government monopolies on trade, government control, government quotas, exchange reductions, exchange regulations, control by administrative regulations, and control by deals within integrated international corporations. All these things, or indeed any one or two of them, could be as important today to trade, if not at times more important, than tariff levels themselves.
Since world war II considerable progress has been made in removing some of those obstructions. As the minister knows, they have been gradually removed as Europe recovered from world war II and was able to stand on its feet and look after itself in the realm of international trade. This removal was pretty steady and satisfactory in Europe over the years so far as it went. As a consequence our trade with Europe has increased.
Let us not forget that this removal was largely due to help received from overseas. In terms of income no country, not even the United States, supplied as great an amount of help for that purpose, for an enlightened self-interest purpose, as Canada itself. Our record is very good in this field, as I would point out to the hon. gentleman who just preceded me. This is true of our record both in regard to trade, in regard to tariff policy itself, and in regard to association with O.E.E.C.
We were criticized a few moments ago because in 1948, when O.E.E.C. was set up, we did not take advantage of the opportunity to join it and it remained for the present government to convert O.E.E.C. into O.E.C.D.; then to become a full member. If my hon. friend who was dealing with this matter had done more research he would have known perfectly well that in 1948 it was quite impossible for Canada to become a member of a strictly European organization and which we desired at that time to remain a European
3970	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy organization. It was only after Europe recovered over the years and got a stronger foundation for its economy that it was possible to convert it into the organization we have today.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: And the United States was not a member.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
And, of course, the United States was not a member at that time. We both were observers during those years. If an offer had been made-and certainly suggestions were made during those years-of full membership it would not have been possible to accept it.
There has been progress on this international front but that progress has been, I think, if not slowing down in recent years, replaced by the development in the world of regional organizations. We know all about them. We talk a good deal about them in this house. Of course the most important of those regional developments is one that we sometimes think of only in terms of politics. The most important is the communist ideological and trade region which is centrally controlled and directed from Moscow at this time, with perhaps some assistance or competition from Peking. There is central control of trade within this bloc. This is one of the reasons we should be more interested now than ever in an Atlantic trading community. Control of trade within this communist bloc is exercised for the benefit of the Soviet union. If any member in this house wants some interesting information on this score let him read the history of Yugoslavia during the period when Yugoslavia was trying to break away from the international communist trading bloc.
Control of competition within the bloc is exercised by Moscow as well as control of communist penetration in noncommunist countries. This is done as much for political as for economic reasons. Indeed, this whole question is a sector of the cold war. If the communist regional trading bloc wishes to send MiG's to Cuba they will accept sugar for those aircraft, but only on their own terms; and those terms will be dictated, when it is necessary, by political rather than economic considerations.
Well, this is one trading bloc we have to take into consideration when we consider this subject. Others are the trading blocs growing up in Latin America, especially in the Central American region. These may be more important in the future than they are at the present time. But what we have in our minds, particularly when we talk about trading blocs, is European trading blocs. They have been referred to previously in this debate.


Ten years ago the European common market was considered a quite unrealistic dream. It is now a going concern, a reality, and it is making startling progress to the point where all trade obstructions will soon be removed, every kind of trade obstruction, among the members of this community. This is being done in a very successful way, partly -and this has a very important bearing on our own problem and the problem of the Atlantic trading development-because it is being done gradually stage by stage. European development is facing exactly the same kind of problem that we would be facing in this country and in other countries of the Atlantic area if we were trying to build up an Atlantic economic community. Five or six years ago some of these problems were considered almost insoluble by the members of the European economic community. I am thinking of the preferential arrangements for overseas suppliers, and of the problem of agricultural imports both within the community and between the countries of the community and outside. I am thinking of capital development programs and the necessity for adjusting special situations to the reduction and the removal of tariffs.
The European countries faced those problems. They were certainly problems. Their difficulties were just as great and just as far reaching as the problems we would be facing in the Atlantic community if we had initiated and were successful in bringing about that wider kind of development. The European countries have been successful up to the present. They are taking their time; it is a 10 or 15 year process. In the period that has elapsed since they began this process the trade increases within the boundaries of the countries inside that community have been absolutely spectacular.
We should not forget also that in this development, up to the present at least, consideration has been shown to the interests of countries outside the community. In spite of some statements by ministers about the dangers from this development, it would seem that those dangers have been taken into consideration by the members of the European community themselves. If we do a little less preaching and a little less whining and make an effort to adjust ourselves and associate ourselves with this development, we shall get further in regard to protection of our own trade.
In that regard I am thinking, for instance, of the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in Paris. This was his entry into the international economic lists as Minister of Trade and Commerce. He went to Paris last December and he is reported as having

said, in regard to this development which I have just talked about, namely the European common market:
Unless the European common market substantially reduces its announced tariff schedules affecting imports from Canada at the GATT negotiations in progress in Geneva, Canada will retaliate by increasing its barriers against imports from the six European countries.
Could there have possibly been a more untimely and unwise statement; that unless the European economic community reduced its tariffs against Canadian imports, Canada would retaliate? Well, the European economic community did not fall for that kind of bluff, as we know. But up to the present at least it has taken into consideration the interest of outside countries. Indeed, the first tariff reduction inside the community was extended to all outside countries.
This development of the European economic community which is of such great importance to us that it has been paralleled by the development of the European free trade area. All those other European countries which had not been willing or able to join the common market have formed a free trade area of their own, and in that regional association we have our most important customer next to the United States, namely the United Kingdom. But the United Kingdom in the free trade area has made it quite clear and there is no use of our whining or preaching about it, that it is going to move across the channel and, if it can, make arangements for association with the European common market.
It is very important, of course, for Canada to protect her position to the maximum possible extent in the face of these developments. Naturally we have to do that. Naturally we have to take every step we can to persuade the European countries that this coming together, which is desirable, should be on a basis of expanding trade with the outside world rather than restricting trade. But surely we can do that, as I hope to point out, by adopting a positive rather than that negative kind of attitude which has been adopted more than once by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Particularly by the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
The speech of the Minister of Finance at Ste. Adele is the one that is always very much not only in our minds but in the minds of commentators on this continent and in Europe. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the positive approach to this problem is that the closer Europe gets together politically and economically the better it will be for the free world, including Canada. This can be done, Mr. Speaker, and I hope it will be done, by the
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy European countries without disregarding the interests of their friends or their own wider interests. I am thinking, of course, particularly of our commonwealth of nations.
This common market, scoffed at as a Utopian dream 10 years ago, is now, as I said, a growing concern, and the members of the European free trade area are increasingly moving toward integration with it. That trend is now clear, and no words by members of the government inside or outside the house, in Paris or Ste. Adele, are likely to stop that trend.
Mr. Macmillan made this perfectly clear during his recent visit to Ottawa and Washington, just as the United Kingdom lord privy seal, Mr. Heath, made it clear two or three months ago, I believe, in Geneva. The United Kingdom is moving across the channel and seeking a basis for membership in the common market. It now feels, according to its spokesmen, that for this purpose satisfactory solutions can be found for the three important problems standing in the way; and if they can be found for these problems affecting the United Kingdom, solutions can also be found in the wider area of Atlantic trade for the problems affecting the United States and ourselves. These three important problems are commonwealth preferences, agricultural imports and political sovereignty.
Canada, the Canadian government, in fact any Canadian government, should face this fact and face it as an opportunity to be exploited rather than a menace to be prevented or a development to be complained about. Certainly the President of the United States has faced it and has accepted the development. He said on February 16 that he welcomed the move, and I quote from his statement at that time:
We shall support and encourage the movement toward European integration.
Then he added these important words with reference to European integration:
It can contribute greatly to meeting the goals of the broader Atlantic community.
Indeed, our own Prime Minister in earlier days has talked along these lines of the development of the broader Atlantic community. The vice president of the United States, in a very carefully prepared and considered statement in Paris on April 6, had this to say:
If that cohesion and capacity-
Of the Atlantic coalition.
-is to be enhanced, vigorous measures will be required in the political, military and economic fields. Our end goal... should be a true Atlantic community in which common institutions will increasingly be developed to meet common problems.

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in his recent visit confirmed that this is the position of the United Kingdom also, when he said at Boston:
I have no doubt of what our aim should be. We ought to try to work for the largest area of free trade that we can create.
This is the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. He went on to say:
Free trade for a free world. That may still be a vision. It may be a long time before it can take practical shape ... Yet many new and vital ideas are now being discussed by practical men which a few years ago would have been dismissed as impractical dreams.
Then he went on to say that one "new and vital" idea he had in mind was an Atlantic trading area. He invited Canada, the commonwealth and the United States to assist and encourage, rather than to shy away from and discourage, that development. The lord privy seal in his speech last February was even more specific in a special point which is always brought up by those who are hesitant about or opposed to this development They talk about commonwealth preferences, and we know the importance of commonwealth preferences in our development over the years. But we also know that commonwealth preferences are a very different thing now from what they were 15, 20 or 25 years ago. Certainly that is the way they are now con-considered in the United Kingdom. I know that the Minister of Finance has expressed some very strong views about the retention of commonwealth preferences, but this is what the lord privy seal of the United Kingdom said about them on February 27 last:
Britain would have no objection to a reduction of the preferences that her exports enjoy in commonwealth markets if the Six wanted to start negotiations with the commonwealth to that end.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that Canada should be in the very forefront in starting such negotiations rather than hindering them. We should encourage European economic as well as political integration on a basis of expanded, not restricted, trade, and then we should do everything we can to convert that European economic community into an Atlantic trading area with which, stage by stage, other free countries could be associated.
There are only four courses open to us, Mr. Speaker. I have already put them on the record of the House of Commons, and I hope the house will forgive me if I put them on the record very briefly again today, because they have certainly been pointed up by developments since I last spoke on the subject.
The first of these policies is to work for the maximum of economic self-sufficiency, that is economic nationalism, the kind of economic nationalism we had from 1930 to


1935 under the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. This might have some tempting short run attractions, especially in a time of recession. In spite of the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce it seems to have some tempting short run attractions for him, when he talks about creating jobs for people in Turin and not for people in Canada. Presumably we should take action which would prevent those people obtaining jobs, so there can be more jobs in Canada.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the lessons of contemporary history and contemporary politics show that you cannot export unemployment in that way. When we have 705,000 men out of work at this time perhaps it is tempting to say, "Let us keep these goods out and we will put all these people to work". But that is running counter to the whole trend and development of contemporary international economic policy. We know now or we ought to know that we cannot export unemployment in this way, and that if we try to do so we will add to unemployment instead of reducing it. That is why we on this side are opposed to that solution. There is no salvation here.
The second possible alternative policy is economic integration with the United States in a continental free trade area. That was well put forward not very long ago in Toronto by a very distinguished American, Mr. McElroy, a man with a great deal of governmental and business experience. It may be, although I hope it will not be, that under certain circumstances we will be forced to consider that solution. If there is, and I hope there will never be, economic disintegration within the commonwealth; or if the European countries come together in a European area which excludes us or from which we on this continent have excluded ourselves, and if the procedures under GATT begin to slow down and eventually break up, then we will be forced to consider continental solutions to our problems.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, that should be a last resort for one reason especially, namely how could we keep our separate political identity in such a situation? When the Minister of Trade and Commerce says, as he said in this house yesterday, that the proposal we are putting forward in this amendment and the proposals we have put forward outside this house-he quoted me in that connection- mean that we are supporting free trade or a commercial union with the United States, he shows he has no understanding whatever of what we mean when we talk about the development of an Atlantic economic community. This has no bearing whatever on 1911 or reciprocity. I suggest the minister

do a little reading and thinking on this subject. Perhaps if he would not spend so much time cheerleading and shouting slogans he might retire for a change, as it has been put, into the lonely recesses of thought.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: And contemplation.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Contemplation might be a little bit too much to expect.
Now, the third alternative is a policy of continued reliance on GATT as the international agency for broadening the area of freer trade throughout the world. As I have said, since the war GATT has undoubtedly been the major agency for the reduction of obstructions to trade. I think the previous Canadian government and the present Canadian government have done everything possible to continue that process under GATT. I think Canada has played a very good part in GATT. However, we cannot help but ask ourselves whether GATT can do much more in this direction, and whether we should not, at least as something complementary to GATT rather than opposed to GATT, take a hard look at regional development. Perhaps the current discussions which I believe open next week on GATT, in which the European common market will take part, will give us the answer to the question of whether GATT is the agency on which we have to rely for further real progress in this international economic field. In my view a new impetus is now required, and that can be given without contradiction to GATT by the Atlantic countries themselves.
This, Mr. Speaker, brings me to the fourth and best alternative. I refer to the careful, steady, stage by stage building up of an Atlantic economic community. This is not going to be done in a week or a month or a year. It is going to take a long time. During the process of development the same steps will have to be taken to protect industries that are immediately affected by these developments as are being taken successfully in Europe today in respect of industries which have been affected by the European common market. This can be done, and it should be done, over a period of five, 10 or 15 years. This process of adjustment can take place and the government, by its action and by its assistance, can participate in that program so that international economic progress will not be at the expense, in so far as it can be avoided, of individual national industries. This is what I mean, what we mean on this side, when we advocate the development of an Atlantic trading community.
I know all the difficulties in the way. I have mentioned them many times in this
Alleged. Lack of Trade Policy house. But I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that there is any other solution to our international economic and perhaps our international political difficulties. There is no solution which will be big enough and deep enough other than the one I have just mentioned. The important thing now is to get this process started.
This is a matter of political will more than economic argument. This government had a wonderful opportunity to begin that process in 1957 when the United Kingdom made an offer of free trade between the two countries, about which we used to hear so much and about which there has been a great deal of silence lately. Even as late as 1958 the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom said, while in this country, that offer was still on the table. It is not on the table any longer; it has been brushed under the rug.
But that was the time when we in this country could have started this process. We could have said to the United Kingdom that immediate free trade between ourselves is impractical and free trade among the Atlantic countries at the present time is impractical, but the two of us can start at once to discuss the building up of an Atlantic free trade community in association with those regional developments which are now taking place in Europe.
Who knows, Mr. Speaker, what might have happened during the intervening three years if that had been the stand taken by the goverment at that time? It is not too late now, but it may soon be too late if the European common market completes its development, and the introduction into it of the European free trade area is successful. It may be too late to bring about conditions for a wider common market if no action is taken on this side of the Atlantic. We on this side, even at this stage, ask the government of this country to take an initiative in this regard and show some of the vision now about which they talked so much three or four years ago.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those who have been in the house this afternoon have listened to a repeat performance of the speech delivered yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition in Toronto. I think we will agree it has not improved with repetition. However, those who sat in the house yesterday to hear the speech of the hon. member for Laurier in introducing his amendment heard a speech which has few equals in the house as a compound of misrepresentation and distortion of the government's position and record.
If the opposition wishes to put forward a policy and wishes to praise the policy it puts

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy forward, no one can take exception to that course, although we will reserve the right to reply to it. Evidently, however, it is necessary, when the hon. member for Laurier puts forward a position on behalf of the official opposition, to take account of the weaknesses and frailties of the case he is putting forward, because he grossly misrepresented and distorted the government's position and its record. He put up straw men yesterday, Mr. Speaker, which bore no resemblance to the government's positions; and he proceeded then, following typical Liberal tactics, to talk out of both sides of his mouth at the same time and to utter contradictory statements.
In so far as there is time today I shall endeavour to put the facts concerning the government's record and the government's position before the house in contradistinction to what the hon. member for Laurier put forward yesterday. I shall deal with the subject discussed by the Leader of the Opposition, and I shall measure what these hon. gentlemen have said against the record of the Liberal party in this regard.
The amendment, Mr. Speaker, invites the house to express condemnation of the government because it says the government has not followed a consistent policy. Mr. Speaker, I say to you that the government has followed, in relation to trade and our international financial policies, a vigorous, dynamic, consistent, forward-looking, balanced program of action.
The amendment does violence to the truth. I endeavoured to state the aims of the policy of the government in relation to trade in 1958 in the first budget speech, and I put it in these terms:
First, to achieve expansion, diversification, better balance and greater stability in our trade with all countries.
Second, to extend and strengthen Canada's trade and economic relations with the commonwealth.
Third, to support and promote a regime of law, order and morality in the field of international trade; to respect the spirit and intent of international commitments and to stand ready to defend our rights and interests if they are challenged or ignored.
Fourth, to recognize the legitimate needs of Canadian procedures; and to safeguard them against unfair trading practices.
Fifth, to promote the balanced growth of all sectors of Canadian industry and agriculture.
That was the declared policy of this government in 1958. That is the declared policy of this government today, and it is a policy that the government has consistently followed throughout.
In keeping with this policy we have endeavoured to assist Canadian exporters to extend their markets and win new markets abroad. Gratifying successes have been gained in our efforts to secure the elimina-

tion of discriminatory trade barriers erected against imports from dollar countries after the war, and in promoting the convertibility of sterling and other major world currencies. Within the past two and a half years sterling and other European currencies became convertible and the great majority of discriminatory restrictions against dollar imports have been eliminated. Canadian exporters are now finding readier access to world markets than at any time since the war. To these highly beneficial developments I say that the efforts and the policies of the present government have made an effective and commendable contribution.
Let us think back to 1957 and the situation to which this government fell heir when hon. gentlemen opposite and a good many others left the treasury benches for all time. First, Canada in those days had an adverse balance of trade on commodity account of nearly $1 billion. In 1960 that adverse balance had been reduced to $100 million. Today we have a better balance and a better diversification in our markets throughout the world. These are substantial improvements.
Our trade with the United Kingdom has increased very materially. Our trade with the commonwealth has increased; our trade with Japan has increased. Those restrictions which had been imposed in the war and post-war years by many countries for balance of payments reasons we did our best, by persuasion and in conferences immediately after we came into office, to remove. Substantial progress has been made in that regard and very great consequent advantages to Canadian exporters have been achieved.
The international monetary fund was in existence, but with general support on the part of member countries, including strong support from Canada, the resources of that beneficent institution have been substantially enlarged.
The same is true of the resources of the international bank for reconstruction and development. An international development agency has been born out of the international bank for reconstruction and development, with a capital of $1 billion. This is an institution to which Canada gave important support in the international proceedings which preceded its birth.
As to GATT, this organization has unquestionably been strengthened by the support that has been given to it in the four years since the change of government.
In relation to the customs tariff of this country, studies have continued and adjustments have been made in it following references to the tariff board, in all cases in accordance with the letter as well as the spirit of GATT.

There have been many conferences designed to promote an expansion of trade. There have been conferences within the commonwealth. The first of them was held here in Canada at the end of September, 1957. This was the first time the finance ministers of the commonwealth had met in Canada, and important decisions flowed from that conference.
The monumental commonwealth trade and economic conference held in Montreal in October, 1958, achieved a large measure of agreement among all the commonwealth countries, notwithstanding the diversity of their interests. That, I think, was an eye-opener to the whole world.
It has since been followed by very beneficial results throughout the commonwealth. The system of commonwealth preferences has been upheld and the benefits that Canada enjoys in that regard-for which much is owed to the foresight of the late R. B. Bennett -have been strengthened and Canadian producers have enjoyed those benefits.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we come to more recent events. We have had many conferences with the United States. There have been bilateral conferences at which problems in the trade and economic field have been discussed in a spirit of mutual understanding. Benefits have flowed from those meetings.
Then there is the organization for economic co-operation and development which was born in 1960 out of O.E.E.C. There was no point in the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) in which he did greater violence to the truth, unless it was the speech made yesterday evening by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) which so completely misrepresented the position of this government in relation to O.E.C.D. If there is any government among the 20 member nations of O.E.C.D. that played a strong supporting role in bringing about the transformation of O.E.E.C. into O.E.C.D., it is the present government of Canada.
There were no such things as export credit institutions when we came into office. There are now facilities available to Canadian exporters of capital goods to find credit in Canada to assist in their export operations. Never before in Canada's history had there been an export conference like the one called by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), last autumn. This was something new; this was breaking new ground. Evidently it had never occurred to those who today occupy the front opposition benches yonder.
Behind the effort to maintain and extend Canada's markets there has been invested more drive and more vigour under the present
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy government than ever existed previously. Benefits have accrued to all Canadian producers and exporters.
When we came into office the premium on the Canadian dollar in that summer of 1957 rose to six cents, and this placed a very heavy burden upon Canadian exporters. It is a very difficult problem; it is a hard thing to move; but we have done our best and we are not at all displeased that this premium has now been reduced to about one cent, with very great consequent advantage to Canadian exporters.
Hon. members opposite talk about flexibility. Well, they did not show much flexibility except in the way they handled the truth in this debate. We have shown at all times a consistent and dynamic approach to trade questions and a full realization of the importance of maintaining and expanding Canada's markets abroad.
This is not simply a short range policy; this is our continuing, consistent and long range policy. We have pursued it diligently and consistently. We have always shown ourselves ready to talk trade. There have been many bilateral discussions. There have been many missions. These have all had as their objective, and many of them have resulted in, the maintenance and expansion of trade.
We heard something said yesterday about GATT. We heard some very distorted remarks about GATT. I have said in previous debates -and I shall not delay this debate to repeat such remarks today-that this government has given consistent support, not merely to the institution of GATT, not simply to the terms of the GATT agreement, but to the spirit of GATT.
We have observed that at all times it is a great mistake to think that GATT is an inflexible instrument. It is not. GATT could not have survived if it had been utterly inflexible. GATT does make provision for amendment; it does make provision for the fact that circumstances may change in a dynamic world trading community, and it makes provision for changes according to certain procedures. Where such changes have been sought by the Canadian government they have at all times been sought in accordance with the procedures laid down in GATT. Never has there been a departure from the provisions of GATT. As to all the proposals we have submitted to the house in three annual budgets in relation to tariff changes, most of these have been preceded by very thorough investigation and study on references to the tariff board. So let us have an end to this nonsense about casting doubt, as the hon. member for Laurier did yesterday, on the sincerity of members of the government in their support of GATT.
3976	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
The principle of GATT is the principle of multilateral trade which seems to have lost its interest for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). The Liberal party now is evidently turning its back-it has at least turned its shoulder-against GATT. It has lost interest. Let me tell the Leader of the Opposition that it was the present Canadian government, through its representatives, which insisted at the discussions in Paris, the three conferences which led up to the formation of O.E.C.D., on the preservation of the principle of multilateralism as laid down in GATT. It was due as much to our efforts as to those of any other country that GATT was called in and was represented at those conferences.
We heard yesterday from the hon. member for Laurier some flights in the realm of fiction with regard to the government's position in reference to tariffs. The hon. member talked about high protectionism. Evidently he does not know what high protectionism is, or he prefers to talk in fictional terms. I shall not delay the house by repeating what I have said before, that this charge is baseless. This charge which has been made by the official opposition in the amendment in this regard is false. I hope I have made my meaning clear. Whatever we have done has been done in accordance with GATT and in accordance with suggestions and reports by the tariff board. While I do not say this is the final and only test, it is relevant to point out that out of 392 items changed in the Canadian tariff by the present government in the course of three budgets, formal changes of mixed character number 203, increases number 65 and decreases number 124. I despair of an end ever coming to the misrepresentations of the government's position to which hon. members opposite have turned.
In 1958, I recall-and we were reminded of it yesterday by the hon. member for Laurier-there was a modest tariff change introduced following the report of the tariff board in the customs duty on woollen fabrics. One would have thought, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) that the end of all creation had come-that we were going to be visited with retaliation by any number of countries. Well, the house has learned long since to realize that the hon. gentleman excels in this kind of matinee performance.
But one expected something more serious of the hon. member for Laurier. Certainly he has gone a long way since he left Cornwall, or since Cornwall left him. Gone is his interest in seeking some measure for a decent chance of survival for the textile industry. Yesterday he returned to the Bonavista-Twil-lingate line of 1958 and talked about the legislation of that year, the amendment to the [Mr. Fleming (Egllnton).l

Customs Act. He misrepresented it yesterday and said the government took power to make arbitrary changes in the tariff rates. The government did not do any such thing. Amendments were introduced to see to it that power was given to prevent the dumping of goods from abroad into this country at prices below the cost of production. This is the kind of unfair competition which hon. members opposite expect Canadian producers and Canadian workmen to face. What do they care?

speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
I shall have to ask the hon. member to reserve his question until I have finished. I shall be glad to deal with it then, but time is precious and limited today.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate told us at that time we were going to face retaliation from Italy. What happened? Our exports to Italy rose substantially in the following year. So much for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He was so worried about the export of codfish to Italy. He sees a codfish behind every shadow. Well, our export of codfish increased, too, so the hon. gentleman was running true to form. The fact is that this legislation well served its purpose; so well, indeed, that it was not necessary to pass orders in council enabling the minister to make orders under it. Foreign exporters knew very well what they would face if they attempted to dump goods on the Canadian market at less than the cost of production and governed themselves accordingly. That is why it was not necessary to make orders under that legislation. This enactment served a salutary purpose.
The hon. member for Laurier yesterday talked about the government following a policy of timid protectionism. At that time I asked him the simple question whether he thought the 1958 legislation was worthy of support or not. He has not seen fit to answer that question, yet he talks about timidity. He ran, and he has not stopped running yet. He roared yesterday like a mouse.
Let me pass on now to say, in relation to the tariffs and to GATT, that we are engaged in the discussions at Geneva at the present time which were detailed yesterday by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). Some hon. members opposite still do not know the nature of discussions up to the present time, and these proceedings have been more protracted than was expected. The discussions so far have been concerned largely with working out with the six members of the European economic community an agreement in relation to their common external tariffs. Now, at Geneva, the

countries represented are about to engage in what has become known as the Dillon round of negotiations. These are the negotiations in which an effort is made to negotiate further mutual concessions. This is an entirely different operation. May I say this: what has been said here by the ministers in relation to what has been going on at Geneva has had a salutary effect.
The hon. member for Laurier yesterday asserted that if the Minister of Finance was sincere in saying he was a strong supporter of trade on a multilateral basis, "the Canadian delegates at Geneva must surely have presented concrete and bold proposals for freer trade in the world." He was referring to the Geneva meetings but he evidently does not know that these negotiations have not even begun yet. His timing is away off. But that is not all. His statement totally misrepresents what has been going on at Geneva, and I could add much more to that if there were time.
I am concerned about the Liberal flight from GATT, for they have evidently decided to desert the ship. The hon. member for Laurier took some satisfaction yesterday in quoting the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition in Vancouver in January, 1958, when he said:
In short, it seems that the era of gradual tariff reductions through GATT has come to an end.
Well, things have not come to an end just because he has ceased to be a minister of the crown. Then, in Toronto, last night, in a preview of the speech he made here this afternoon, the hon. gentleman is reported in the Ottawa Citizen as follows:
Mr. Pearson questioned whether GATT could do much more than it has done already.
If the hon. gentleman wants to fold his hands and say "all is up" let him do so. That attitude of resignation, that attitude of inaction, is one that he has inherited typically from the government of which he was a member. That is not the attitude that this government takes. This government proposes to make its loyal contribution to this beneficent international organization in the manner in which it has for the past four years.
Then they quoted the Ste. Adele speech. I feel flattered, but they did not seem to quote enough of it. They picked out bits here and there and then proceeded to put their own fancy interpretation upon them. Let me put a couple of facts straight for their instruction. In the first place that speech I made at Ste. Adele last autumn brought substantial benefit and assistance to our negotiators at Geneva in the negotiations in which they were then engaged.

They had not started yet.
25, 1961
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: That speech assisted negotiators at Geneva.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: They had not started yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they are all mixed up, the poor fellows. I pointed out that the earlier negotiations were the first round of negotiations at Geneva to work out agreement in respect of the new common external tariff with the European economic community, and that is where it was established.
That is what this Ste. Adele speech was designed to deal with. The hon. gentlemen opposite-perhaps I should not call them poor fellows, but I have a soft heart-did not realize that was the nature of the first round of negotiations last year. I may say that the declaration at Ste. Adele did help to strengthen the hands of the Canadian negotiators at Geneva in the first round of tariff negotiations there with the representatives of the six countries constituting the European community.
I must now pass quickly over some other subjects. First of all, in relation to our trade with the United States, I say that we are achieving a better balance. We were concerned that so much of Canada's trade was in one basket when we rame into office. We have been able to move some distance, not by trying to restrict trade in any direction, but by trying to expand trade. The expansion of trade has shown itself in striking form in our trade with the United Kingdom, the commonwealth, Japan and many other areas in the world. My colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce last night drew attention to the extraordinary increase in our trade with the United Kingdom in the past year, which reached an all-time record for Canadian exports to the United Kingdom. We take a good deal of satisfaction in this and congratulate all those enterprising Canadian exporters who took advantage of the opportunities that were opened up in the market, at least partly as a result of the negotiations carried on by the present Canadian government.
These conferences that I have referred to produced very beneficial results. I shall not deal with that aspect. I think I should, however, say a word on the subject of preferences because the Minister of Finance has a responsibility in relation to Canadian imports and to the Canadian tariff. The policy of this government has been at all times to seek the full enjoyment for Canadian producers, and particularly for Canadian agricultural producers, of all the benefits available to them under commonwealth preferences. These are very important benefits.

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
So far as our trade with the United Kingdom is concerned, here are some facts that I invite hon. members opposite to ponder. First, about 95 per cent of Canadian exports to the United Kingdom enter that market duty free. Forty per cent of Canadian exports to the United Kingdom enjoy the benefit of preferences. For most of these, but not all, the preferential rate is free. Of our total exports to the United Kingdom in 1959, 39 per cent were primary industrial materials free of duty from all sources. That is to say, there was no preference. Forty one per cent were agricultural products. The largest agricultural item, wheat, does not enjoy preference. Oil seeds, coarse grains and tobacco are the principal agricultural exports which do enjoy preferences.
On 7 per cent of our exports to the United Kingdom the creation of E.F.T.A. will result in the loss of significant preferential advantage over other E.F.T.A. countries competitive with Canada in the products involved.
At the commonwealth trade and economic conference in 1958 this subject was considered by the representatives of all the commonwealth countries. In the report of the conference, article 28:
-reaffirmed the importance of the role that preferences have played and continue to play in commonwealth economic relations. Commonwealth countries have continued to adhere to the preferential system while adjusting their policies to the requirements of changes in the scope and character of world trade.
In article 31:
The United Kingdom government confirmed its intention of maintaining as an important element in the preferential system the free and unrestricted entry of nearly all goods imported from the commonwealth.
We have waited until today to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) indicate in his lighthearted and happy-go-lucky way that it does not matter very much about these commonwealth preferences. He has indicated that these advantages are not going to have very much of a place in his thinking from now on. They still have an important place in the thinking of the Canadian government when we realize the advantages that these preferences have offered to Canadian producers and above all, to the Canadian agricultural producers. Hon. members opposite can forget their duties and responsibilities to the Canadian agricultural producer but as far as the present government is concerned it intends to remain faithful to the interests of the Canadian agriculturalists.
I come now to our trade relations with western Europe. These are of very great importance to Canada. Over the years, 30 per cent of our exports have gone to western Europe, including the United Kingdom. We


do, with the seven countries, now eight, of E.F.T.A., twice as much business as we do with the six countries of the European economic community. Here again the member for Laurier could not present his case without distorting and misrepresenting the position of the government. He said that the government was opposed to the European common market. I am being charitable to that hon. member when I say to him that he does not know what he is talking about.
At the commonwealth finance ministers' conference at Mont Tremblant in 1957, the ministers reported that they "reviewed the progress made toward the ratification of the treaty of Rome, establishing the European economic community, and the effect of this treaty on the interests of the commonwealth. They noted that the treaty would receive further consideration in international organizations.
The United Kingdom ministers reported on the progress made following the United Kingdom initiative for the establishment of a free trade area in Europe. The commonwealth ministers recognized that the establishment of an outward-looking free trade area in Europe would broaden the advantages to be derived from economic integration in Europe, not only by the United Kingdom but by all other participants. This was regarded as important as it could contribute to agreed commonwealth policies of expanding world trade.
It was also agreed that there is need for effective machinery for continuous consultation among commonwealth countries on matters related to the European economic community and the proposed free trade area.
The United Kingdom ministers reaffirmed the undertakings previously given by their government about the safeguarding of commonwealth interests in the United Kingdom market for foodstuffs, drink and tobacco."
That was the position in 1957. The commonwealth countries expressed their concern over any movement at that time of the 14 countries toward the formation of a European free trade area and suggested that care should be taken not to prejudice the interests of the commonwealth countries in relation to their exports of agricultural products to the United Kingdom market.
The United Kingdom ministers gave assurance that they would not prejudice these markets in their negotiations with a view to bringing about that European free trade area. Things went forward on that basis until December, 1958 when efforts to bring about this wider European free trade area came to nought at the meeting in Paris.
It is not for us to apportion responsibility for the failure of that effort. The fact is that the effort to form a European free trade area

was made under the terms upon which it had been discussed at these commonwealth meetings, and had been harmonized with the interests of the commonwealth countries. In the face of those assurances as to the position of the Canadian exporters in the market of the United Kingdom, we had no fear.
What happened in 1959? We saw a widening of the rift between the Six and the Seven in Europe, and we expressed concern, as one of the member nations of NATO, that there should be developing in Europe an economic rift, and this was a matter for deep concern. When the hon. member for Laurier said yesterday that we were opposed to the European common market, Mr. Speaker, he did violence to the truth. Our concern at all times was that in any move in the developing trade pattern of organizations in Europe the interest of the commonwealth, and particularly of our own Canadian producers, for whose interest we are responsible, should not be prejudiced thereby. We saw opportunities there for the development of that organizational pattern in Europe without working prejudice to the opportunities enjoyed by Canadian producers either in the markets of the United Kingdom or in the markets of those European countries, as long as the policies and attitudes of those countries were outward looking and not inward looking. The great concern has been that in the development within the European economic community-perhaps in the other organization as well-outward looking policies may be supplanted by inward looking policies, and while reducing the barriers to trade among themselves, they might at the same time erect higher barriers around the perimeter. This has been our concern and any Canadian government worthy of its trust would, Mr. Speaker, in a situation of this kind, do what the present Canadian government has done. It would be vigilant; it would go to every meeting that was called for this purpose, and it would put the interests of the Canadian producers before the conference and in a spirit of reasonableness at all times, not the spirit of retaliation that hon. members opposite so mistakenly and misleadingly talk about, seek to bring about a harmonization of interest that will do justice to and safeguard the interests of Canadian producers. That is our responsibility and our trust and we will fulfil it.
What about the moves of the United Kingdom in the direction of a common market? Well, Mr. Speaker, we are talking about something that is still very tentative; indeed, in some respects, hypothetical, because it is perfectly clear that the government of the United Kingdom is not prepared to join a European economic community on the basis
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy of the treaty of Rome, and so far the government of France has given no indication that it is prepared to consent to any modification of the terms of the treaty of Rome with a view to providing accommodation of the British in the European economic community or with other countries of the European free trade area. So, when we are talking on this subject let hon. members opposite be frank enough not to talk about this as though it were something assured. Let them be frank enough and informed enough to talk about it as though it were what it is, something very tentative, indeed, and hypothetical in many respects.
In this situation, Mr. Speaker, having regard particularly to the assurances that have been given to us by the government of the United Kingdom, that the commonwealth countries will be consulted at all stages, and while it remains the undoubted responsibility of the British government to make its own decision, we shall, of course, having regard to Canada's interest both in the United Kingdom market and in the markets of those European countries, seek to preserve the benefits that we now enjoy while at the same time recognizing the importance of the expansion of those markets and the benefits that will flow to Canada from them.
We have taken no narrow view here, Mr. Speaker. There has been the grossest kind of misrepresentation on this subject as to the position of the government. We never threatened retaliation in the meeting in London last November; we never threatened retaliation in Paris in 1960. These statements are distortions; they are figments of the imagination.

speechtext: Read the Ottawa Journal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Read the editorial in the Regina Leader-Post and in similar Liberal organs. That is the source of the information. I am giving them the needed information; I am telling them for their information, but I suppose it will fall on unhearing ears, that their assertions are quite untrue. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I have been at those conferences and never has there been a suggestion of retaliation in my hearing. But we have done our duty in warning those other countries that if a course were taken which had the effect of closing Canadians out of certain markets, then inevitably Canadians, being enterprising people, would be looking for markets elsewhere, and trade being carried on in the world under arrangements which are so often negotiated, undoubtedly large sections of Canadian producers would expect the Canadian government to negotiate favourable terms of entry in other countries, and this is unquestionably

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy the position in which we find ourselves. We have to take action if that is a possibility and that is why we have been so vigilant in this field.
In my concluding remarks let me say first of all that in so far as O.E.C.D. is concerned, the government takes unlimited satisfaction out of the active part that it played in bringing about the O.E.C.D. Far from hon. members opposite adopting this convention as though it were theirs, let me say to them that the present government throughout has conducted those negotiations and it is not going to be any help to deny to the O.E.C.D. now the use and the prestige that this organization needs when the Leader of the Opposition in effect did invite the countries concerned to sidestep the O.E.C.D. and in effect weaken it.
I have said that our concern at all times is for the maintenance and expansion of Canadian markets; but we do not propose to be parties to any narrow approach of the kind that is proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, if he is to be taken as meaning what he has said, what he is in effect proposing to do is to forswear and abandon the principle of multilateral trade for which Canada stands. He is proposing that Canada and the other countries of the North Atlantic area should turn their backs upon trade with countries such as Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Africa and other countries and resort to discriminatory arrangements, resort to more restrictions or, in the Nelson tradition, to keep one eye closed. Our view, Mr. Speaker, is that we want in all respects to see outward looking policies pursued, not restrictionist policies. If the kind of policies that the Leader of the Opposition has talked about were followed, if he means what he says-and I cannot persuade myself that he means to go as far as his words have conveyed to his hearers-it would mean that Canada would be held within the closed area of the North Atlantic, and that would not be good for Canada.
