speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during the time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was speaking I could not help but recall that during the period 1930 to 1935 I frequently had occasion to sit in a very different part of this chamber. In those days the policy of the then prime minister, the Right Honourable R. B. Bennett, was to blast his way into the markets of the world. Well, today, the policy of the present government has been clearly set out by the Minister of Finance. It is to bluster its way into the markets of Europe.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: Bluster, rave and misrepresent.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: The extent of the misrepresentation of the Minister of Finance can best be illustrated by his reference to the amendments to the Customs Act of 1958, when he said there had been no orders issued under that act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: You did.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: You said it had not been necessary.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
The minister said it had not been necessary to issue orders. I want to point out that on April 18 his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), as appears on page 3776 of Hansard, had occasion to apologize for the misrepresentation that had been made and pointed out that there had been a great many orders issued. He himself had made the same kind of misrepresentation and he was very quick to correct it as is fitting in keeping with what should be the manners of a minister of the crown. The correction was made in the presence of the Minister of Finance but he persists in the misinformation today.
I could go on correcting the Minister of Finance but I presume I should make my own speech. I should like to point out that the Minister of Finance seemed to be bolstering the achievements of the government by his manner and the loudness and vigour of his voice today. That is his privilege if he wishes to do so, but he kept referring to these achievements as momumental achievements of the government. I would simply point out to him that tombstones are monuments and maybe he is building a tombstone for our trade by means of the wrong policies of the government which he neglects to correct and replace with proper policies.
The minister went on to take credit for some reduction in the exchange rate between Canada and the United States. Some of us read the minister's speeches on occasion, and this is the same Minister of Finance who always disclaimed previously that the government could do anything about exchange rates without the imposition of foreign exchange controls. He took great care to point that out on other occasions but today he takes credit that the exchange rate is down a little. May I remind him that the famous baby budget, which presumably he is claiming is the factor responsible for this reduction, did not seem to bring down the exchange rate because it went up after the delivery of that infamous speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: No, it did not. It went down.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: It went up.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: You made a lot of miscalculations in that budget, didn't you?

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
The record will speak for itself. Another inconsistency of the minister in his remarks today had to do with the figures as to the numbers of items with respect to which there had been increases or decreases in the tariff, since the present government took office but he took great care in the figures he gave to omit the dozens of tariff items affected by the legislation finally passed last week. Those items were omitted. They were just not included in the computation.
Perhaps I might point out other inconsistencies on his part today. He talked about the European common market being tentative.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: I did not. I talked about the approaches.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: Did you know what you were talking about?

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Perhaps I might elaborate by saying that he talked about the approaches to the common market being tentative. I must point out to the minister, however, that however tentatively he views these things they are not tentative but very real in the mind of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, as he made clear in his speech in Boston and many other speeches he made while he was on this continent.
Perhaps I should put the amendment on record again at this point because I fear it has not been fully understood. Certainly the Minister of Finance during the whole course of his speech tended to put an interpretation on it that misrepresented its content and purport completely. The amendment is in these words:
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets the protectionist and inconsistent trade policies of the government and its failure to develop a long term foreign economic policy to enable Canada to participate fully in the challenging new opportunities in the field of international trade by implementing a vigorous program to promote the expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries and by encouraging the development of an Atlantic economic community."
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) moved the following subamendment:
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma and by adding thereto the following words:
to prevent a drastic loss of overseas markets for agricultural and other primary products."
I regret that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is not in his seat at the moment because, however true it may be that the failure of the government to develop a long
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy term foreign economic policy to enable Canada to participate in the new opportunities in the field of international trade and its failure to encourage the development of an Atlantic economic community may result in a drastic loss of overseas markets for agricultural and other primary products if we do not succeed in relating ourselves properly to these new developments, there are other consequences as well. While the loss of overseas markets for agricultural and other primary products is of major importance in this whole debate, it is only a part of the total picture. The effect of the subamendment is to limit and restrict the amendment, and I would point out that the effect of this limiting and restrictive addition to the amendment is quite diffierent from the speech of the hon. member moving it.
It seemed to me from his speech that he did not mean to limit his approval of the amendment in any way but the fact is that by the words he has used in the subamendment he has tended to limit the amendment. While I grant at once the extreme importance of the matters he has referred to in the subamendment, the words he has used have a limiting effect and therefore the subamendment is not acceptable so far as we are concerned.
Incidentally, he made an implication with reference to me in his speech which I should like to dispel at once. There should not be read into the amendment any lack of interest by me in any part of it. I am very keen about the whole of the amendment and just as much in support of the reference to secondary industry, as I hope to show later in my remarks, as anyone in the house. He is quite wrong in any deductions he made because of the amendment being proposed by one much abler than I. I assure him that this was done because of the desire and readiness of the Liberal party to work together and to have the amendment moved on this occasion by one of prime ability.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: Do not be so modest.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Unfortunately the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) has vanished, but I should like to make some references to the speech he delivered yesterday which I must admit I found rather interesting because it demonstrated the very thing about which we are complaining. I want to read one excerpt from the minister's speech. In talking about the main motion-I presume he meant the amendment-he said this as reported at page 3945 of Hansard for April 24, 1961:
It purports to speak on the one hand of a free or freer trade area within the Atlantic economic community and in the same breath it expresses
3982	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
regret because, it says, the government has failed to promote the expansion of secondary manufacturing industries in Canada. These two courses are contradictory and represent opposite ends of the economic pole.
There, sir, you have an expression of the policy of the government, that there is an inconsistency in these two things. Surely, the contrary is the fact and it is important that we do both of the things proposed in the amendment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, by that negative view, is going to leave us in a position where we would take a retrograde step and we would thereby become purely producers of primary products. Surely, that is not the government's position and yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce has clearly set it out in that way in his speech. I must say, however, that his speech of yesterday was consistent with his other speeches on this precise point.
The purpose of the amendment is to suggest, first, the failure of the government to develop a long term foreign economic policy. It seems to me that in today's world it is not good enough for the Minister of Finance or any other minister of the crown, in answering this amendment, to try to deal with it in terms of days long past. It must be dealt with in today's circumstances, today's world, and it must be dealt with in the context of the cold war which, it seems to me, is being developed more and more on economic terms. In that context, surely it is elementary that the free western countries must be brought to a consideration of the prospects of trade, a subject that ought to be foremost in our minds.
I recognize that certain short run considerations are important from time to time in the consideration of external trade. I quite recognize the day to day vicissitudes of trade and I am not one to minimize their importance. However, this amendment is concerned with long term foreign economic policy. We are concerned with the development of this long term policy over the years ahead so that we will provide the proper trading climate in the years ahead. The Minister of Trade and Commerce completely missed that point yesterday. He talked about certain trade figures, merchandise trade figures for this year and last year, without relating them to this important point.
Then, we have this problem of the government-I am making this as a direct criticism of the government in every area-being hypnotized by this short run, day to day view. The government seems to be unwilling to develop long term policies. Surely, an able government must do both. It must be able to develop long term policies as well


as be able to look at the day to day problems. Our need now, in our external relations, is for a long term foreign economic policy.
I do not want to traverse ground that has been traversed. My leader made an excellent speech on February 28, which appears at page 2499 of Hansard, on the subject of O.E.C.D. I will not repeat any part of that speech now. However, there are aspects to this problem which time does not permit me to develop, which are very beneficial for Canada and for the whole free world. I refer to such matters as the expansion of trade with underdeveloped countries and the reliance of those countries on certain commodities with sharply fluctuating prices, with a resultant adverse effect upon them. I should like to develop that theme on some other occasion, but perhaps I will have to let it go with a mere mention now.
If we should develop an Atlantic trading area on a really sound footing, it would do much to stabilize prices of the basic commodities which come from these other underdeveloped countries. This would be a very good thing as anyone knows who understands the sharp reverses their economies have had.
The Minister of Finance today seemed to go out of his way to deny certain impressions that were created by his remarks, and more particularly by the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I could, perhaps, spend a good deal of time quoting the remarks of the Minister of Finance, especially from his speech at Ste. Adele. I thoroughly read again this morning the speech delivered at Ste. Adele. I was interested to note that the minister did not attribute to that speech the quotations he made from it today. He read a substantial part of it into the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
I read it again this morning to see if I had misinterpreted it, since the minister is so quick to challenge my original interpretation. However, my original interpretation still stands. I have a whole sheaf of quotations from the Minister of Finance here, but perhaps I will content myself by reading one from the Toronto Globe and Mail

of November 22, which refers to this Ste. Adele speech. The minister is reported as saying:
Canadian interests will be damaged, perhaps seriously, if the United Kingdom aligns itself with the common market countries in some sort of free trade area. Canada might retaliate by raising its own tariffs.
The article goes on to state:
Certainly under such circumstances the pressure for Canada to embark on closer trade associations with other countries, particularly the United States, would understandably be increased.
Evidently the correspondent for the Globe and Mail interpreted the speech the way the rest of us did.
Then, on November 25, there were some questions asked in the house about this speech at Ste. Adele. The minister persisted, according to Hansard, page 197, in these remarks that we interpret as a threat of retaliation. He will find those remarks recorded at the top of the first column of page 197.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: There never was any threat of retaliation.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: In any event, the remarks are interpreted that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: It is the wrong way.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce went to Paris to deal with some foreign trade matters. He is reported as having stated-it depends on which paper you read, but all the reports are of the same nature:
Unless the European common market substantially reduces its announced tariff schedules affecting imports from Canada at the GATT negotiations in progress in Geneva, Canada will retaliate by increasing its barriers against imports from the six European countries.
The warning has been given by trade minister George Hees to European ministers meeting here ...
There it is. Since this government took office the Department of Trade and Commerce has been truncated. Remnants of it are left with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I hope the jurisdiction he has over that part which is concerned with foreign trade-and it seems to be shared between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance-will be further reduced, if he is going to persist in making ill-timed statements of that sort.
If the minister has any doubt about the interpretation by others of the speeches of this government, I would refer him to the Financial Post of December 10, 1960. This is quite a long article-it covers a full page- by Clive Baxter. The article is headed:
In Europe, they say that Canada overrates her own importance .. .
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
I could quote a great deal of this article; I could quote it all if I had the time. In any event, it reports that Mr. DeGrood the head of the North American division in the directorate-general for external relations at E.C.M. headquarters, who is described as a Dutchman and a friend of Canada, said:
"It seems to us", he finally replied, "that Canada overrates its own importance these days. We want to trade with you, but you must understand that if necessary we can get on without you".
Another part of the article, not attributed directly to this spokesman, says:
It is not encouraging to report-but impossible to ignore-that the speech seemed to worry nobody in Brussels. The departments concerned were interested in its contents but apparently far from scared by its warnings.
"You got yourselves into this mess", commented an E.C.M. executive who didn't want his name used for obvious diplomatic reasons. "We are not to blame for what happened. But please explain to Canadians that while we sympathize with your problems, you cannot scare us with the sort of threats Mr. Fleming used.
"If you don't like what we are doing you are of course free to take whatever measures your government sees fit. But I think you should remember this important fact: We are a unit of 170 million people. We have ambitions to build what may some day be an equal of the United States in every respect.
"Much as we like Canada and Canadians, don't ever think that a market of 17 million people can threaten us into changing our basic plans. We will listen to your views and where possible will meet your requirements, but please don't lose your sense of proportion. You are going to have to live with us in the future and to withdraw into an angry protective shell can only mean worse and worse trouble for your economy".

Exactly. It is just the same kind of inconsistent trade policy illustrated by the minister when he spoke about the Cubans, when he went on with that kind of

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy nonsense and said, "You could not wish to do business with better businessmen anywhere". Those are the kind of irresponsible and careless statements we are getting from the ministry. Those kind of statements have consequence in our international trade relations and ought not to be made in the brash, thoughtless way in which they apparently are being made.
I could digress and list a great many famous boo-boos made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but of course it is not desirable to do so at this time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext: They have made a complete volte-face since then.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
They would need to make a complete volte-face since then. Not only has the government done nothing appropriate about these long term policies that are required at this time, but their short term policies are regressive. It is quite clear that these policies will cause a good deal of trouble for our secondary industry in the time ahead. They have already caused our secondary industry a good deal of trouble.
In giving the figures yesterday for commodity trade the Minister of Trade and Commerce completely missed the significance of some aspects of this matter. He did not tell us that our imports were down because of the recession in business in this country. He did not tell us that our exports to the United Kingdom have increased-and we all rejoice in the fact that they have increased-because there has been a sharp upturn in the economy of the United Kingdom. He did not tell us that this year there was a very significant feature in our increased exports to the United Kingdom; in that about 5 per cent of it represented wholly manufactured goods.
The minister did not relate the significance of that fact to the possible development in this country of secondary industry, which this government is doing so much to destroy. He did not-

speechtext: That is nonsense.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROMOTE SECOND- ARY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
In dealing with the other items, he did not deal with the true significance, in long term effect, on the economy of the country. The minister merely dealt with them as if no long term factors at all were involved. He did not deal with the threat to our agricultural products, which apparently was in the mind of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam if the European common market develops into a protectionist association. The minister did not deal with that matter at all.
He did not tell us the danger we must meet in this regard. When the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) was speaking last


night, I could not help thinking how little he understood the danger and threat which exists to our wheat exports in certain of these movements that are going on wholly outside Canada and outside direct participation by this country. The hon. member seemed to have missed that point.
It seems to me that the two parts of this amendment are wholly consistent. In addition to developing policies by way of negotiation with these two European trading associations in order that we will be integrated in a proper association with them-as was so ably expounded by my leader this afternoon- we have the other problem. I refer to the problem of our secondary industry and its development.
The present government has made much of the baby budget delivered last fall. It is interesting to see that the President of the United States saw fit to refer to it in his message to congress. Unfortunately, I have only the newspaper reports. I would like to see the text of the president's speech. However, it is quite clear that he may already have started the chain of events which will be damaging to the economy of this country that our Minister of Finance initiated by his angry, little, wrong policies in the baby budget. In any event, the present government has failed to realize the effect of the whole of the taxation policies of the last few years and has failed to realize what they are doing to the economy of this country.
In face of the rapidly changing conditions in the economies of Europe, Japan and other countries in the world the government has failed to understand the necessity for adapting our tax policies in such a way as would provide incentives for our export industries so that they can remain competitive. It has failed to realize the role which a government can play in this field. It has failed to realize the importance of adopting tax policies, whether by tax incentives or otherwise, which would enable our secondary industry to provide itself with the most modern machinery and equipment. That is the direction which our taxation policy should be taking. Instead of that, the government has been following policies which have increased the burden placed on our export industries and lessened their ability to compete successfully in world markets. I refer to its misunderstanding of how to handle the conversion loan with its indirect consequence of an increase in municipal taxes on industry and a higher interest rate on money borrowed. Corporate income taxes have been increased. The sales tax has been increased to 10 per cent. Old age assistance tax has been increased by 50 per cent and the unemployment insurance charges on

industry have been increased by between 25 per cent and 50 per cent depending on which category is involved.
All this has constituted a very heavy burden on our productivity, a direct addition to the cost of production and, indirectly, an added burden on our productivity. What is required now is an adaptation of these tax policies, every one of them, on a broad and massive front, to meet the needs so that we can once again put secondary industry into competitive production. Then we would not have these policies of fear and the retaliation which these two ministers go around talking about outside the country.
We have had in this country an excellent experience of using accelerated depreciation allowances to facilitate the transition of industry from a wartime to a peacetime basis. That policy was used to great advantage and I am at a loss to understand why in the circumstances in which we find ourselves today the government does not use this vast experience which has proved itself so effective in past years, applying it to the changed problems and requirements of today, because the need to help industry develop and increase its productivity is as great today as the need of industry for help to convert to peacetime production was then.
There are many other phases of taxation to which I could refer and upon which I could elaborate but I see I have only four or five minutes left. The corporate taxation field is neither a popular one to speak about nor an easy one, and I do not wish my remarks to be considered as meaning only that we should take the easy step of reducing corporate income taxes. It is a matter of developing all the taxes which affect corporations in a way which will relate particularly to the export problem. That would involve certain adaptations of the sales tax policy and it would also involve the use of depreciation allowances. It would involve an examination of the techniques of releasing earnings from companies for investment in new and up to date equipment. It might also involve an examination of the right of shareholders to withdraw their dividends on a more advantageous tax basis than is presently the case. It will involve some wholly new policies.
It was suggested by the Leader of the Opposition on January 20 of this year during the budget debate as reported at page 1274 that special provision might be made in the field of earnings from increased exports. My hon. friend spoke on this very point in a precise way and made a suggestion of a particular nature:
To encourage domestic manufacturing industries to increase their exports tax incentive should be
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy offered including a reduction in corporation income tax on the profits earned on increased export sales.
There are a great many variations in the forms of tax incentives that could be offered. In any event-

speechtext:
I should be obliged if the hon. gentleman would bear with me one moment and ask his question at the completion of my time.
These things are not being done by the government. Instead, it is taking retrograde steps each session in this whole field of taxation. The speech made last night by the Minister of Trade and Commerce showed a complete failure to understand the nature of the problem facing this country in the field of foreign trade, both as to its long term implications and as to its short term relationship to unemployment and the difficulties facing our secondary industries. We have sought in this amendment and in our debate to put forward criticisms of the government but to accompany these criticisms by positive and responsible suggestions capable of being carried out and, which, if carried out, would render wholly unnecessary these debates on unemployment which take place so frequently in the house when a Conservative government is in office.
These suggestions, if adopted, would eliminate the need for these parades of unemployed to parliament hill seeking to make representations to members of parliament. All these things would become wholly unnecessary. As I say, in criticizing the government we have sought to accompany our criticism with a program of the kind that should be carried out by any active and responsible government in this field and to demonstrate exactly how these policies would work. However, I am afraid the present government has closed its collective mind to any ideas of a progressive character. Hon. members opposite seem to think in terms of turning back the clock, and it is for that reason I referred at the opening of these remarks to the bluster of the present Minister of Finance and to the blasting into the markets of the world spoken of by the then prime minister of that party some 30 years ago when unemployment was as much of a worry as it is today.
Mr. J. R. Keays (Iles-de-la-Madeleine).
Yesterday we heard the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) move an amendment in this house which demonstrated again his ability to create the paradox of paradoxes. He criticized this government for either the lack of a trade policy or an inconsistent trade policy, while in the same breath he mentioned

Alleged, Lack of Trade Policy that there was an expansion of trade under this government. However, he found ways and means for not giving credit to those Canadians who are imaginative and possess initiative and drive. Rather, he gave credit to the dynamic growth of western Europe. In other words, he again expressed the opinion that Canadians were lazy, lacked imagination, initiative and drive.
It seems to me that in addition to preaching doom and gloom hon. members opposite are trying to destroy confidence in Canadians. In an article appearing today in the Canadian Manufacturers' Association pamphlet there is one sentence which seems to refer to that which I have just mentioned. That article suggests that public confidence in the immediate future should not be undermined or disturbed by playing up the bad and playing down the good in such a way as to distort the over-all economic picture and thus promote fear and doubt where there should be none, which would do Canada and the unemployment situation a great disservice.
As I have mentioned, hon. members opposite do not give any credit to the initiative of the government. However, some people think that the action and policies of this government in so far as trade is concerned are quite satisfactory. In an article appearing in the Citizen of December 14, 1960 under the heading "Golden Decade Has Lost Much of its Glitter" Mr. Ben Dworkin had the following to say:
In the meantime the drive by the Canadian government to secure outside markets is believed to be a factor that will give business generally a boost.
Despite the competition for world markets, trade envoys from all parts of the world that are attending a conference in Ottawa report that Canada stands a good chance to break in, or improve her position as an exporting nation to almost every part of the world.
This drive for business, and the enthusiasm that has been shown by businessmen for the program all reflect optimism that new customers can be found.
There is one person who appreciates the policies of this government in so far as trade is concerned. We heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) yesterday refer to the 9 per cent increase in the volume of our export trade since 1957. This is due to the selling efforts of this government, the initiative of those ministers concerned with the problem, and to the selling ability of the personnel we have stationed all over the world. Again, we can speak about our trade imbalance which has gone from $368 miUion in 1957 to $97 miUion in 1960. I believe that these few facts speak well of the trade policy of this government.

Trade problems are growing and the United States last year voted extra millions of dollars to put more salesmen into world centres. The United Kingdom has taken similar action. This proves that the problem rests not solely in Canada but all over the world.
The objectives of the O.E.C.D. are ideal. Let no one believe that these objectives will be reached simply by the stroke of a pen. Many obstacles will be encountered by those members who form O.E.C.D. in so far as trade policies are concerned. Trade talks and horse trading will still go on not only within that zone but with those exporting nations who are desirous of continuing trade, and by the bloc countries desirous of exporting their surplus products.
The O.E.C.D., made up of 20 nations, does not represent the ultimate in respect of western trade, but its immediate objective was aimed at expanding economic aid by the industralized nations to the underdeveloped nations of the world. Canada along with two other countries-! believe they are Switzerland and Sweden-gained the compromise that after the O.E.C.D. was formed it would review the acts of the old O.E.E.C. in so far as trade was concerned. The O.E.CD. also gave all the signatories the opportunity to air problems in respect of general trade policies with a view to protecting them in relation to the defence of trade practices, when a member nation desired to bring forward a trade problem.
These are the concessions obtained by this government. As the Minister of Finance has so ably said, Canada is always aware of the problems which may arise with other trading nations and must at all times protect herself.
To substantiate my statement about the organization, which included a number of the common market members, I would refer to what Mr. Ludwig Erhard said as reported in the Gazette of January 25, 1961: under the heading "Erhard Fears 'Tragedy' of European Split":
Mr. Erhard's restiveness about the common market is founded on his conviction that it is cementing an economic split between its members and the rest of Europe. He regards this as an economic and political tragedy and considers that it weakens rather than strengthens the free world.-
The weight of Mr. Erhard's declaration lies to a notable degree in the intangibles of the situation. Despite his affirmation of loyalty to the written treaties, it is evident that more than technical observance of the treaties will be needed to maintain the common market momentum in future years.
Although this organization is ideal, there are problems to be surmounted. I am sure this goverment is aware of them and is protecting itself accordingly. Canada does not

wish ideals but rather a commercial relationship with all its trade partners without forgetting the social or political effects of such association.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have criticized the government for failing to take advantage of opportunities for closer collaboration with other members of the North Atlantic community. Some of the hon. gentlemen opposite have chosen to cast doubt on the value of our participation in the organization for economic co-operation and development. To me this reveals a surprising lack of understanding of the significance of this most important step toward co-operation and collaboration among the 18 countries of the western community and the two North American powers.
I think hon. members of the official opposition show extraordinary lack of judgment, consistency and respect in representing O.E.C.D. in an unfavourable light. So short is their memory that they fail to see the contradiction in their taking this stand. Do they not recall the North Atlantic treaty which was signed in 1949? Do they not recall the insistence of the Liberal government, then in power, on the insertion in the text of the treaty of article 2, which reads as follows:
The parties will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and wellbeing. They will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
We have frequently heard the Leader of the Opposition speak on this subject and we know the part he played in preparing the report of the committee of three of the North Atlantic council on ways and means to improve and extend NATO co-operation in nonmilitary fields and to develop greater unity within the Atlantic community. Let me ask hon. gentlemen opposite what the Liberal government did between 1949 and 1957 to develop unity within the Atlantic community in non-military fields? We see no evidence of their having made any progress in this connection. We see no evidence that article 2, through the efforts of the Liberal government, was made meaningful. I think this is sufficient proof of the cynicism and hypocrisy of hon. members of the official opposition in suggesting that they do indeed support the idea of an Atlantic economic community.
This government has moved positively in assisting in the formation of an O.E.C.D. comprising the members of this community. Let it not be for the opposition to imply that we have been as negative or as negligent as they were when they held office.
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
In so far as the subamendment of the C.C.F. party is concerned, I do not think any additional words are required. I think the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) ably answered the problems brought out by the subamendment.
In so far as trade policy is concerned, has this government not moved forward since 1957, bringing in at each session legislation which enable Canada's trade policies to rank among the best in the world? Has it not under the productivity council made it possible for studies to be undertaken and an examination made of the reasons for unemployment? I am sure that if answers are found by this council they will be brought to the attention of the appropriate minister.
Has this government not extended the Export Credits Insurance Act? Has it not made available through the banks sufficient credit to enable our exporters to continue and improve their businesses? Has it not been the policy of this government to make money available to the exporters? Since this Conservative party believes in free enterprise, the government has left to the banks the responsibility of providing exporters with the money they need. The policies of this government are farsighted, vigorous and energetic. We all remember the smug complacency of the previous government. It failed to recognize the problems which were eventually surmounted.
I should like to refer to a few facts which prove that the policies of this government are an encouragement to Canadians. In this respect I am speaking about our secondary industries, because it is in those industries that we will find the answer for unemployment. They alone can give work to approximately 70 to 75 per cent of the Canadian labour force. Our policies have brought some results, as they have made it possible for Canadian manufacturers to compete in other markets. One company I have in mind is a firm called Hamilton Clamp and Stampings Limited, which is challenging two big United States industries which are exporting automotive parts to Canada. This firm has appointed a distributor in New Zealand and negotiations are under way for distributors in Australia and the United Kingdom. It is branching out in the export business with an extensive line of hose clamps that has become its mainstay.
A Swiss backed metal firm has located in Canada, and there are numerous others which have come here because of our trade policies. The Liberals have encouraged their pet project, free trade, by importing cheap goods to the disadvantage of Canadians and resulting in the closing of factories. They have ignored the change in our economy and are in favour

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy of the traditional trade patterns which were in existence in Canada when they were in office. John Meyer, writing about the Liberal party in the Gazette of Thursday, December, 15, 1960, had this to say:
It is only now showing evidence ol concern about the extent of foreign investment in Canada. Had there been the open-mindedness to recognize the dangers of excessive foreign investment in its contemporary form, instead of assuming it to have been in its traditional form, concern about it would have been expressed in the early fifties instead of after the peak has been reached.
What applies to monetary policy, Mr. Speaker, also applies to Canada's trade policy. In those days when there was no question of unemployment, when Canada developed huge surpluses every year, the Liberal party remained smug and complacent. Those were the days when they should have introduced the legislation which the present government has introduced in the last few sessions. If they had done so, our gross national product would not have stopped growing. The impetus would have been given at that time, which was the proper time, in order to keep our national product growing.
There are some Canadians who think well of the policies of the government. William F. Shelley, president of Canadian General Fund Limited, is one. I have here a newspaper article which reads in part as follows:
William F. Shelley, president of Canadian General Fund Limited and co-chairman of the committee of Canadian investment companies, said government action has already stimulated housing construction by liberalizing loans and placed the Canadian automotive industry in a more favourable position through increased duties on foreign cars. Shelley also told the fund's stockholders that the government has succeeded in increasing domestic production by affording further tariff protection and has provided long term stimuli for Canadian exports through new financing procedures.
I think that these actions by the government are commendable and I cannot see how we can support an amendment such as that moved by the Liberal opposition.
Other people also think well of the trade policies of the government. I should like to refer to a report of a speech by Mr. Roberge, the president of Banque Canadienne Nation-ale, at the last annual meeting of shareholders. The newspaper article reads in part as follows:
Mr. Roberge declared that a compromise between the "sixes and sevens" was likely, and Canada's interests might be hurt. "Our exporters must be in a position to face foreign competition, particularly that of the common market which from now on will share with the United States the twofold advantage of modernized equipment and a vast domestic market," he said. Mr. Roberge described the federal government's budget moves to encourage the development of industry and domestic investment "as a first step in the right direction". When


experience has shown their effects, he said, a more comprehensive economic policy would be needed to aid the formation of capital.
That is exactly what the government has done, Mr. Speaker. It has created the productivity council and it is going to establish a design council. These organizations will help the government to introduce proper legislation so that our trade with all nations will continue to grow for many years to come and not, as suggested by the opposition, for just a few years. Again, I do not see why we should have to import finished products simply so we may sell our raw resources. We need protection for secondary industries and, as I have said before, these are the industries that put Canadians to work. The paradox of the Liberal party seems to be that they say we should import more and sell more and at the same time they forget the development of our secondary industries which are so important to the Canadian economy.
So far as the tariff structure is concerned, the Minister of Finance has certainly made a move in the right direction when we realize that not since 1907 has our tariff structure been overhauled. The government is doing something about it because it wishes to make it adaptable to the present and the future. In the words of the Minister of Finance, this will provide an opportunity for a further reduction in world trade barriers and new opportunities for Canadian exporters.
How can the opposition criticize these objectives of the government, Mr. Speaker? Finally, may I say that I endorse fully the steps which have been taken by the government with respect to our trade policies, increasing our export trade and, more important, developing our domestic trade. We have not forgotten the one or the other but have made them all into one common problem which will be resolved by the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) is comparatively new as head of this department, he looks and acts as though he was born for the job. From the first day of his appointment he has taken his job seriously and initiated some innovations, which we all trust will mean more business for Canada, such as the big conference of trade commissioners from abroad, some 110, I believe. I understand that this effort was worth while. Now we are all waiting for the results and I for one wish to congratulate the minister on his enterprise.
Trade is the life blood of our nation and without it we cannot hope to thrive and prosper. But with all the energy of the minister and however great his zest may be and that of his assistants, we can never hope

to gain foreign markets unless we have a favourable trade climate. This can only be brought about by legislation designed to attract foreign buyers and if we do not have it then all these efforts will have been made in vain.
Recent legislation, notably that granting the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) power to redefine for tariff purposes goods of a class or kind made in Canada or that could be produced in Canada, certainly will not create an incentive for wider trade with foreign nations, especially those which are already good customers and purchase from Canada far more than we purchase from them. This measure, fought by the opposition every step of the way, will not help the minister to realize his aspiration to increase and promote exports.
I do not think this country can afford to provide an increase in tariff protection against a surge of foreign competition for manufacturing industries which supply only a small share of the Canadian market. Unfortunately it seems that the new minister is handicapped by the tariff and monetary policies of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), as was his predecessor, now Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill). The latter was handicapped by the obstinate refusal of the Minister of Finance to introduce measures to lower the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to its counterpart, the United States dollar. As he pointed out this afternoon, however, the dollar has dropped to about 1 per cent above par. Now, we see a repetition of this intrusion with the advent of new protectionism which is nothing more nor less than the old Tory protectionist medicine. I daresay that the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe, when minister of trade and commerce, would never have allowed the minister of finance of the day to introduce legislation that would hurt our chances of selling abroad.
A brilliant member of the press gallery, in an article which appeared in the Port Arthur News-Chronicle some time ago, saw how the wind was blowing and had this to say. I quote:
''Trade or perish" would be an apt and pungent solgan for Canada. It is commonly said that one third of all Canadian workers owe their jobs to our trade with foreign countries. This proportion is infinitely higher than that pertaining within the borders of our greatest supplier and our greatest customer, the neighbouring U.S.A. It is probably higher than in any other country in the Atlantic community.
This reporter then goes on to point out that we are building Canada into a defensively-walled trading citadel isolated on a lovely high priced plateau. Then he proceeds as follows:

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
On December 16 Mr. Fleming told the House of Commons that he and the minister of trade, Hon. George Hees, had recently signed, on behalf of Canada, the convention establishing the organization for economic co-operation and development known as O.E.C.D.
The aims of this newly constituted organization, Mr. Fleming told the house, are "to promote policies that are designed:
(a)	to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth in member countries,
(b)	to contribute to sound economic expansion in member and non-member countries, and
(c)	to contribute to the expansion of world trade ..."
Just words, words, words.
O.E.C.D. is a revised version of O.E.E.C., which was just another mantle under which politicians and bureaucrats could "swan" to international debates at the taxpayer's expense despite a consistent record of absolute failure to create even one additional job for Canadian workers.
Two hundred and fifty million citizens of western Europe have decided that small national trading units do not offer an open gateway to mass prosperity and high living standards. So they have agreed to join together in tariff-free economic alliances. These two European groupings, destined one day to amalgamate, are known as the inner six and the European free trade association.
Who are we, eighteen million Canadians, to know better? Yet we have failed to negotiate our entry into either of those prosperous blocs, and we even rejected the offer of a free ride in by Britain. Today, we are not even exploring that golden pasture; we are just signing conventions agreeing to talk, talk, talk.
Now Mr. Speaker, few people would question the soundness of these observations, nor could anyone doubt that the principal cause of the problem is the imbalance of our trade with other nations. Our exports are not sufficient to meet the goods and services which we import and to meet the payments on our foreign debt. There is also a growing body of public opinion, which is substantiated by visible evidence, that Canada is suffering from duplication of production facilities for articles which have only a limited market when divided amongst the numerous participants. This situation leads to lower individual production which, in turn, causes higher prices to meet those costs and those higher costs invite imports, thus bringing new competitors into the production field to divide the small market that exists.

Representatives of the electrical manufacturers were asked by Senator David Croll of Toronto to comment upon this observation. One of the manufacturers of refrigerators, Westinghouse president, Mr. J. D. Campbell, readily agreed that there were too many companies in the business, while acknowledging that it was difficult for him to be objective. He said there was a total market in Canada for 350,000 to 400,000 units a year, while at a conservative estimate the Canadian manufacturers had enough capacity to produce one million units.
Mr. H. D. Style, president of John Inglis Company Limited and English Electric of Canada, said the same situation existed in a number of other domestic industries. He said their production capacity was sufficient to more than supply the total Canadian market, a varying share of which was now going to foreign manufacturers.
Of course, I am not suggesting that we should set up controls and prevent any company from entering any manufacturing field. It is entirely up to them. On the other hand, Canadians should not be asked to pay a higher price for commodities, which would be the result of giving increased tariff protection to inefficient, small producers, who in all probability would soon be back asking for still higher tariffs.
We certainly do not advocate cut-throat competition; nor is it our duty to ask the people, the consumers, to pay the higher prices which higher tariffs would impose.
Contrary to the common belief that high tariffs protect Canadian industries, in reality, in most cases it has the direct tendency of inviting retaliation in kind.
I am fearful that as a result of a shortsighted policy on trade and tariffs, while we may keep out a few thousand television tubes made in Japan, we may jeopardize the sale of millions of bushels of wheat to that country which, incidentally, has a large trade deficit with us. Japan's chief import from this country is wheat, a commodity of which

Canada has a huge surplus. Other commodities which Japan buys from us are the products which directly benefit hard pressed industries such as coal and iron mines.
We should also remind ourselves that we are not the only wheat producers in the world; but in its trade and tariff policies this government acts as if Canada were the only source.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) devoted a considerable portion of his speech to the absurd assumption that the members of the oflicial opposition were against buying Canadian.
I wish to remind hon. members of this house in general and the minister in particular, that on February 11, 1960, as will be found in Hansard at page 952, I urged the government to give consideration to the advisability of sponsoring a "buy Canadian" campaign. I said:
In view of the hundreds of millions of dollars being spent importing into Canada automobiles and consumer goods of a kind already made here, has the Department of Trade and Commerce given any consideration to sponsoring a national campaign to make Canadians "buy Canadian" conscious?
The then minister of trade and commerce, now Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill), replied as follows:
I doubt the urgency of this question, Mr. Speaker. The problem of encouraging Canadians to buy goods made in Canada is one which is of importance, and that type of campaign has been going on under the auspices of business organizations for some considerable time.
I followed up the question by asking whether the Department of Trade and Commerce had given any consideration to a national campaign sponsored by the government, and the minister replied:
There is no consideration being given, at the moment, Mr. Speaker, to a national campaign under the auspices of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The hon. member's suggestion will be taken under advisement.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a very genial fellow and is well liked, but he is also a past master at twisting words around to create different meanings. However, he will not be able to read in my statement anything which would indicate other than that we on this side of the house are just as anxious for Canadian people to buy Canadian as any hon. member of the house, including the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce does not approve of giving any consideration to the proposition of creating a free trade area that would include the United States, Britain, Canada and some European nations.
Mr. R. M. Shaw, senior vice president of MacMillan, Bloedel and Powell River Limited

of Vancouver, addressing the western retail lumbermen's association, made the following statement and I quote:
Canada, if given access to United States markets, would undoubtedly be able to build up a secondary wood products industry to manufacture such products as prefabricated garages, summer cottages and patios, casing sets, overlays, sashes for doors and windows and garden and household furniture.
He said all these products were produced in Canada now but in insufficient volume to take advantage of the economics of mass production enjoyed by larger United States manufacturers.
At present Canada has free entry into the United States only for lumber which has been surfaced on four sides, tongued and grooved. Mr. Shaw believes that under free trade Canada would increase its volume of sales to the United States more than the United States would expand its sales to Canada of similar products.
On the broader aspects of free trade, Mr. Shaw said an outdated degree of nationalism was threatening to isolate Canada from free trade areas evolving in Europe. He said Canada should display the leadership in the free world trading community that is expected of us as a major trading nation.
However, we on this side of the house do not advocate a policy of free trade between Canada and the United States alone. Our leader has made it clear that what we favour is an Atlantic free area which would include Canada, the United States, Britain and other European nations.
Last night, the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to the address of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) delivered to the Empire and Canadian clubs of Toronto on April 24 and I cannot think of a more effective way to bring my remarks to a close than to quote a few paragraphs from it which will indicate the trade policy a Liberal government will establish when the Liberal party is called to form a government-

Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a grievance tonight with respect to a matter which was first brought to the attention of the house on March 14 by

the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel). It concerns a report by a Mr. Hegge who I believe is a business agent for the brotherhood of carpenters and joiners of America. The report had to do with working and living conditions at a federal project at the port of Moosonee. At that time the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said that the matter had just been brought to his attention and that he would investigate it further.
On the basis of information I had been able to acquire I had occasion to discuss the matter further with the minister at that time and he informed me he was sending two officials from his department plus an official from the Department of National Health and Welfare to investigate these very serious charges. After due time a report was made and while the minister did not make the report known to the house he provided me with a copy of it, and my grievance arises out of the complete inadequacy of the report.
To illustrate this point, I think I should list the charges contained in the original news release and say something about their gravity. The news release was made by an officer of the union who professed to have gone to the site and who professed to have gone to the spot. Seldom have I seen a more scathing report than that contained in this release. On examination we find that it contains some 27 specific charges with respect to working conditions, cases of discrimination, false pretences and so on. I think I should list the charges in order to bring hon. members up to date with respect to this matter.
Some of the charges are of a minor nature while others are much graver. However, I think I should list them all because if these charges are true then the minor ones are a part of the over-all picture. The first charge had to do with living conditions and the use of double bunks in a small room, something which was claimed to have been barred from camps of this type for many years. The second charge was that there were no lockers for the men in which they could keep their clothes and personal belongings. Furthermore, there were no doors on the rooms in the bunk-houses and the rooms were open. Only two blankets were issued to each man although we must all realize that at Moosonee the temperature often falls as low as 30, 40, 50 or even 60 degrees below zero.
If I may continue with the complaint, there was inadequate heating, especially in the shower room. There were no shower curtains. There were no laundry or drying facilities. The toilets in this place were broken or there were no seats, and so forth. The basins in the washrooms were not cleaned or sterilized and the floors were never washed. The man who made the complaint said that
25, 1961
Alleged Inadequacy of Labour Report the only time the floor ever saw water was when the sun warmed up enough so that the water formed by melting snow dripped through the leaky roof. There were no safety inspections. There was no first aid equipment in the camp. The men were transported back and forth to work in open dumptrucks when the temperature was 40 or 50 below zero. There was no doctor available to these men, although they were charged medical fees in order to provide the services of a doctor.
There were two charges that might be termed false pretences. It was stated the men were being sent up from the Timmins unemployment insurance office with the promise that they would start at $1.85 per hour with an increase in two weeks. This was not so. Statements were also made that the men would be able to acquire all the overtime they wanted. Again, this was not true. There was a charge that the men were being fined for no given reason. Some of the men, after returning to Timmins, were sent back again and refused employment. These men found themselves without money, and there was no way they could get back to civilization because the trains operated only twice a week. In some cases the men were forced to sell their personal effects or to beg money from the parish priest in order to get back to a larger community.
The men were being fired, as I said, without reason in between trains and their belongings were deposited in the snow. If any hon. member is familar with the number of dogs that prevail in a community like Moosenee he will realize what a hazard it is to have belongings placed out in the snow.
Another charge was that there were no vacation paybooks supplied to these men. This reminds me of a complaint I had last year in connection with this same construction company. The company found a loophole in the regulations and was thereby enabled to flout the intention of the law. It was alleged the company cheated men out of thousands of dollars of vacation pay as a result of this loophole. Evidently a man had to complete a year's work before he became eligible for vacation pay. The weather in this area was such that the men could not work for more than 10 or 11 months, so they never did complete one year of service. Some of these men had had been going back into this area for four or five years, but they never received any vacation pay.
There were charges of discrimination. Carpenters were being paid $1.85 per hour and labourers $1.25 per hour, but both were charged $3 per day for room and board. However, plumbers and steamfitters were being paid $3.47 per hour and they were given free room and board, free transportation and
3994	HOUSE OF
Alleged Inadequacy of Labour Report fare in and out if they stayed six months or were laid off before six months had been completed. The last charge was, irrespective of the fact wages have gone up considerably since 1956, this same company was paying $2.15 per hour for the same type of work back in 1956, with free room and board and transportation. This can be compared with the alleged conditions existing today.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this list constitutes quite a number of serious charges that warrant close investigation. After some three weeks I was supplied with this answer and I think it is only fair to put it on the record in its entirety. I quote:
On being advised by Defence Construction Limited of the complaint concerning certain conditions alleged to exist at the construction camp located at Moosonee, Ontario, the public health engineering division of my department-
That is the Minister of Labour's department.
-contacted one of their engineers who was in the area on departmental business and requested an immediate examination.
This, of course, Mr. Speaker, is contrary to the picture which was given us at the time. We were led to believe the agreement was that Mr. Gordon Cushing, along with another official from the labour department plus one from the health department, would make an investigation of these serious charges. I continue:
With the assistant project engineer of Defence Construction Limited and the project manager of the construction company in attendance, the examination was made on March 15, 1961, with special emphasis being given to complaints brought to our attention. Our public health engineer subsequently reported that no evidence was found to support the complaints.
To be specific, all washrooms were exceptionally clean and free from obnoxious odours. In no instance were there more than two men allocated to a bedroom. Double bunk beds were noted in some bedrooms, but only lower bunks were being used. Considering the traffic involved floors were reasonably clean. At the time of the visit some bedroom floors were being washed by maintenance personnel. The main camp is heated by a central steam system and it was reported that this equipment had not been inoperative during the present winter. Two blankets were issued to each employee, but if desired he may request additional ones.
In general, it was felt that the living conditions in this camp were very good and that the procedures followed to maintain them were satisfactory.
As I stated before, there were some 27 specific charges mentioned in this press release. Out of these 27 charges, two were admitted but it was stated they did not apply. Two charges were evaded. One of these had to do with the heating in the bunkhouse and in the showers. The reply was that the plant had not been inoperative, but that was not the charge at all. The charge was that the heating was inadequate. Two more charges 

were given very suspicious answers. These charges referred to the cleaning ad washing. The reply was that washrooms were exceptionally clean and that the floors were in the process of being washed while the investigation was being made. This statement reminds me of the good old army days when the brigadier came around on inspection. We had at least one week's notice so that we could get everything shipshape before he arrived.
Not one of the other 21 charges was answered or even mentioned. According to this report, the inspection was made but keeping in mind the specific charges that had been made this is either a very poor report of a good inspection or a good report of a very poor inspection. I do not know which. I believe these are serious charges. I do not know whether or not they are true. I think we should know if the charges are true. I feel that the inspection carried out according to the report given to me was certainly inadequate in the face of these serious charges. These charges should be proved or disproved. If these charges are wrong, certainly the man who made them should be condemned for making them. Until such time as the charges are proved false, this situation should be investigated. If these charges are true, some definite action should be taken.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker^ this matter is related to work being done in my riding, so I feel it is my duty to say a word about it. On March 14 I received a letter from Mr. Hegge and I submitted the brief which was sent along with the letter to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). In the afternoon, in reply to a question of mine, he promised to investigate the matter.
I understand that the department has investigated the matter, although perhaps not to the satisfaction of the complainant or the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), However, I wish to inform this house that I have been a member of the Ontario legislature for 12 years and I would not take a back seat to the hon. member for Timmins when it comes to investigating these matters and seeing that employees work under fair conditions, whether it be in camps or construction companies.
The hon. member for Timmins has risen tonight and taken it upon himself to substantiate all the charges that have been made. This shows that the new socialist party has only one hope, which is to try to impress labour that they are the only ones who can talk on behalf of labour and on the protection of labour.
Mr. Speaker, there is one further point I should like to raise, and it concerns the use of information that cannot be substantiated.

If the hon. member for Timmins feels it is right for him to continue with this grievance tonight, even when he knows very well that there are very grave doubts as to many aspects of the complaints, I feel he is not helping these workers, who I hope are enjoying the privilege of working.
With regard to the wage of $1.85 an hour, the hon. member claimed that wages somewhere else were higher in other years. On the other hand, the people who were hired in this area were told by the employment office at Timmins that the rate was to be $1.85 an hour.
In his reply to me dated April 7, Mr. Hegge admitted in the second part of his letter that the rate of $1.85 an hour is the only rate quoted by the Timmins office of the national employment service. This shows that these workers knew they were going to work for $1.85 an hour. Therefore, it seems to me that a member of parliament should take his responsibility seriously enough to not depend on all kinds of innuendos and insinuations to try and prevent people from obtaining employment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) wish to speak on the same matter?
Not on the same matter, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Does the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) wish to speak on the same matter?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I did not intend to speak on this grievance, but I think I should, having regard to what the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) has said.
It may very well be that we in this corner are the only ones who will speak for labour-
You have another guess coming to you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
-and if these charges are made and are to be substantiated, we will certainly take the responsibility for that.
I have talked to a number of people who work in that area and live in the riding of Timiskaming. Many of these complaints have been repeated to me. Unfortunately, it is a difficult proposition to go to Moosonee alone and investigate these complaints. However, I have read the report that was presented to the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin). I agree that the report is not definite, but complaints have been made to me within the last two weeks concerning some of the conditions dealt with in this report, which report indicates that they do not exist.
Alleged Inadequacy of Labour Report
The area of Moosonee is an exceptionally difficult one to get into. For this reason I am sure the hon. member for Timmins particularly stressed this matter of travel arrangements being made for someone who is going to be fired. Certainly consideration must be given to these people getting in and out of the area, because the train does not run every day; three days elapse between going into the area and getting out again. Therefore some consideration should be given to this aspect of the situation, if only because it is such a remote area.
I have been in the bunkhouses that we are discussing. They were closed for several years, with the exception of one that was kept open for the staff in the area. These bunkhouses are now being used again, and conditions cannot be as good as they should be.
I think any hon. member who receives complaints should do something about them. This is also true of the hon. member for Cochrane. If he is the labour representative that he says he is, or tries to imply, I think he has the obligation to go to Moosonee-not I, and not the hon. member for Timmins- because it is in his riding. The hon. member has an obligation to go into Moosonee and investigate this matter. It is a difficult trip; it is 150 miles up and 150 miles back; but the hon. member for Cochrane has the obligation to do that. If he does not show this interest, I think he has very little right to rise and attack another hon. member for having brought this matter again to the attention of the government.
In my opinion the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) should investigate this problem. He should investigate it by sending officials to the area and the officials should not necessarily see the company and have a planned tour. It is almost impossible to get into Moosonee as it is without the company knowing about it, because unless you fly in you have to go to the railway to make arrangements to go there. You have to notify the information director of the railway and arrange for accommodation in Moosonee, because the railway owns the only lodge in that community. Therefore it is almost impossible to go in on a surprise visit.
I think the minister should give full consideration to these charges. He should send a representative of his department into the area. If the prevailing rates are not in accordance with the rates that are being paid in other instances for this type of job in an isolation posting, and if the job requirements are not being met, I think the government has a right to demand from the contractor that wages and conditions be raised to a suitable level.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
