I am not responsible for the minister, and I am not particularly responsible for this grievance. However, I have talked to some of the constituents in my area who are working there, who have told me that conditions are not as good as they should be.
We agree that there has to be some leeway in the type of accommodation that is available in that area, but I point out that one of the other companies in the locality has very good bunkhouses.
The bunkhouses under discussion are very old and are in bad shape. They have not been used to any extent for some years. They have outside, steam heating that runs between one building and another, and in temperatures of between 40 to 50 degrees below zero it is quite legitimate that complaints should be registered against these conditions.
I am surprised that we should be asked to accept a report which indicates, not that the heating is not sufficient but that it had never been shut off for a period of a year. In my opinion that does not mean very much. If it is not adequate it might as well be shut off, because it will probably be very uncomfortable living in this type of quarters.
Again I repeat that if workers across the country have to turn to the C.C.F. and the New Party entirely to handle the type of complaints we have received from Moosonee, we will make every effort to see that justice is brought into this matter.

Mr. Speaker, one thing has been made apparent tonight concerning the particular grievance raised first by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) and later by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel). If anything has been demonstrated tonight it has been the failure of the New Party, the C.C.F., or whatever they choose to call themselves, and the Liberal party to take an aggressive interest in their constituencies whether in the case of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) or his colleagues from the same area. In the face of the unhappy conditions which were described this evening by the hon. member for Timmins it seems to me that any member of parliament in that area who heard about incidents of that kind would have gone into them and examined them. If the people of that area had had the wisdom to elect a Progressive Conservative member this type of thing would have been investigated and rectified.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is the hon. member for York-Scarborough familiar with the situation in which this problem was raised many months


ago? The government was asked to make an investigation into it and it is only recently that the results of the investigation have indicated the unfortunate situation which now exists.
What about the mess at Scarborough?

To reply to the first question first, I have taken the trouble since this grievance was made to examine Hansard. I listened most carefully, as I always do, to the hon. member for Timmins, and if the New Party has this monopoly of concern for the working man-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member has departed somewhat from the grievance, as have one or two others who have spoken. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) has risen on the same matter as the hon. member for York-Scarborough he might as well save his time.

I should like to assure the house that any member of this group will always take up any complaint regardless of the constituency in which it might originate. We consider that as members of this house we are responsible to the whole nation and that we are expected to do what we can on behalf of all the people of Canada.
However, I should like to place on record my sincere regret that after the member for Timmins had risen and announced his complaint the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) should have deemed it advisable to leave the house and has not even been represented by his parliamentary secretary. I should like to place it on record that both of them are absent.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
I had, of
course, no previous knowledge of the matters which would be raised nor have I any definite knowledge of the circumstances which surround the absence of the two members referred to, but I do know that the Minister of Labour was required to leave the house tonight to go, I am told, on official business to the United States. I take exception to the inference as to the cause of his absence made by an uninformed member of this house.

I would have the hon. lady know that I am very adequately informed as to the situation in Moosonee, and I regret that in the absence of the minister it was not deemed advisable to at least have him represented by his parliamentary secretary.

Yesterday around one thousand unemployed marched in Ottawa to meet the cabinet and present a brief to them. I must first of all congratulate the unemployed who came to Ottawa on the orderly manner in which they conducted themselves. They presented a very well prepared brief.
What was the reaction of the members of the cabinet present? First, who were present? There was the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley), and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mon-teith). Out of the five only one was wise enough not to speak, knowing the government could or would not do much more. He was the Minister of Defence Production. He knew, after the declaration made by the Minister of Labour not very long ago, that very little more would be done and he was wise enough not to say a word during the meeting. His colleague had said, of course, that the government having done everything it could possibly do and the rest was in the hands of labour and management.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Were you there?
I take that from the newspapers that reported the proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You should have been there and you would have known he did speak.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: One at a time. Perhaps the hon. member would state his grievance so that we might understand it. I am not sure whether his grievance was that the ministers spoke or that one did not speak.

My grievance is that the unemployed came to Ottawa, they met the ministers, and the answers they received were not equal to the present situation being faced by the unemployed in Canada. That is my grievance. What did the Minister of Labour say or promise? First, according to the Montreal Gazette, the minister said-and this is in quotation marks:
As a government, we don't want this problem.
It is not the kind any government would want to perpetuate.
I certainly admit that no government would likp to perpetuate the kind of situation we have presently in Canada. I want to be fair to the minister. I do not want to believe that the government is not doing the best it can in the present situation. But the best the government can do is not enough for us 90205-6-253

nor is it enough for the unemployed of this country. The government refused for three years to admit there was an unemployment problem. For three years it said there was no unemployment, and the Liberals and the other parties were criticized as spreaders of doom and gloom. The government declined to take action until the situation was out of hand and it could do little about it. Second, the government did not act with sufficient energy and daring when finally it did attempt to do something about the situation. The only thing it came out with was the winter works program.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member unnecessarily but the grievance procedure at this stage permits of the expression of definite single items of grievance. It seems to me that the hon. member is allowing his grievance to range over the whole field of unemployment and action taken in that regard. I understood his grievance related to the reception given to a delegation in Ottawa yesterday. If the hon. member would confine himself to that he would be in order.

My intention is to speak about the way these men were received and the little which was given to them by way of promises by the government. I should like to speak about the way in which the government might have dealt with the matter while this delegation was here. This would cover the question of unemployment to a certain extent. These were unemployed men coming here and wanting help from the government -wanting to have the question settled once and for all by the government-and I think the grievance, put in that way, could be accepted by the Chair.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Message from the Co-Chairmen of the Geneva Conference on Indochina on the Cease Fire in Laos
The co-chairmen of the Geneva conference on Indo-China represented by the governments of the Soviet union and Great Britain are following with great concern the situation which has developed in Laos.
They proceed from the fact that if this situation is not changed the position in Laos may become a serious threat to peace and security in southeast Asia. They note at the same time that real conditions exist for normalising the situation in Laos in accordance with the national interests of the Laotian people on the basis of the Geneva agreements of 1954. The co-chairmen have in view the understanding already reached that an international conference to settle the Laotian problem is to be called in Geneva on the 12th May this year.
The co-chairmen call on all military authorities, parties and organizations in Laos to cease fire before the convening of the international conference on Laos and they call on appropriate representatives to enter into negotiations for concluding an agreement on questions connected with the cease fire.
The co-chairmen call on the people of Laos to co-operate with the international commission for supervision and control in Laos and to render it assistance when it arrives in the country on their instructions in exercising supervision and control over the cease fire.

Message From the Co-Chairmen of the Geneva Conference on Indo-China to the Government of India on Convening the International Commission for Supervision and Control in Laos
The co-chairmen of the Geneva conference on Indo-China represented by the governments of the Soviet union and Great Britain are following with great concern the situation which has developed in Laos.
They note that real conditions exist for normalising the situation in Laos in accordance with the national interests of the Laotian people on the basis of the Geneva agreements of 1954. They have in view the understanding already reached that an international conference for settling the Laotian problem is to be called in Geneva on 12th May this year.
The co-chairmen have addressed to all military authorities, parties and organizations in Laos a call for a cease fire and for the carrying out by appropriate representatives of negotiations for concluding an agreement on questions connected with the cease fire.
The co-chairmen propose to the government of India that it should convene in Delhi the international commission for supervision and control in Laos. They have in view that the commission will discuss the question of the tasks and functions which should be allotted to it after the cease fire in Laos and will present an appropriate report to the cochairmen who will consider the commission's report and give it directions on going to Laos to carry out the work of controlling the cease fire.
The co-chairmen in their message on the cease fire in Laos called upon the population of Laos to co-operate with the international commission for supervision and control in Laos when it arrives in the country on their instructions and to render it assistance in exercising supervision and control over the cease fire.
The co-chairmen are sending a copy of this message to the other two members of the international commission for supervision and control in Laos-the governments of the Polish People's Republic and of Canada.
